entries.question: Does the bible condemn gambling?
entries.summary: Proverbs 23:4 ("labor not to be rich") is offered as a condemnation of get-rich-quick schemes including gambling. The opposite side stacks Numbers 26:52-56, 33:54, 34:13, and Joshua 14:2, 18:6, 19:51, 21:8 — Yahweh repeatedly commands the land of Canaan to be divided by lot (goral), and Joshua casts lots as a method of divine guidance. If casting lots is gambling, the Bible commands gambling.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is structurally weak and the SAB framing is over-reaching. Proverbs 23:4 says al-tiga' le-ha'ashir — "do not weary yourself to become rich" — and is part of a wisdom-tradition warning against pursuing wealth as an end. It does not name gambling, and applying it as a gambling-condemnation requires the interpreter to add the specific activity the text never mentions. The SAB is using a generic anti-wealth saying as a prooftext for a specific modern category.

The casting-of-lots side is on firmer ground but still not quite what gambling means in modern usage. Goral in the Hebrew Bible is a divinatory instrument, not a wager. Numbers 26 and Joshua 14-21 use lots to determine tribal land allotments because the procedure was understood to reveal Yahweh's will — Proverbs 16:33 makes the theological framework explicit: "the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." Acts 1:26 has the early Christians casting lots to select Matthias as the replacement apostle, again as a method of seeking divine guidance, not as a game of chance for monetary gain. Jacob Milgrom's JPS Numbers commentary and Richard Nelson's Joshua commentary both treat lot-casting as a divinatory ritual.

So the SAB has constructed a false contradiction by misidentifying the categories. Proverbs 23:4 is not about gambling. Casting lots in Numbers and Joshua is not gambling in the modern sense — it is sortition for divinely-guided decision-making. There is a genuine biblical lacuna on gambling (the modern category did not exist), and one can argue that wisdom-literature warnings against wealth-pursuit and against laziness do not produce a coherent biblical position on gambling either way.

However, there is a real adjacent contradiction worth noting: the soldiers casting lots for Jesus' garments at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34, John 19:23-24, fulfilling Psalm 22:18) is presented as a wicked Roman act, while the same procedure in Numbers and Joshua is presented as divinely commanded. The act of casting lots changes moral valence based on context, which suggests the Bible's treatment is not principled but situational.

Verdict: this specific SAB contradiction is built on weak prooftexts (Proverbs 23:4 is not about gambling). The lot-casting practice itself is divinatory rather than wagering. A real contradiction exists in the adjacent question of whether lot-casting is divinely sanctioned or impious — but that is not what the SAB is asking.

commentary_out.commentary:
The SAB entry is structurally weak because it equivocates on the word "gambling," and the equivocation collapses under examination of both prooftexts. Proverbs 23:4 reads al-tiga' le-ha'ashir, "do not weary yourself to become rich," continuing with "cease from your own wisdom." The saying belongs to the "Words of the Wise" collection (Proverbs 22:17-24:22) and is a warning against exhausting oneself in the pursuit of wealth as a goal, paired in 23:5 with the image of riches sprouting wings and flying off. Fox's Anchor Yale volume reads it as a counsel of contentment and detachment from acquisitiveness, not as legislation against any specific revenue method. Nothing in the verse names games of chance, wagers, or stakes; treating it as a condemnation of gambling requires the interpreter to supply the very activity the text omits. The SAB is pressing a generic anti-wealth aphorism into service as a prooftext for a modern moral category.

The casting-of-lots material is historically richer but still mislabeled as gambling. The Hebrew goral denotes a divinatory instrument — most likely small marked stones or potsherds — used to disclose a decision believed to come from Yahweh, not a stake risked for monetary gain. Numbers 26:52-56 and the land-allotment narratives of Joshua 14-21 deploy lots precisely because the procedure was understood to remove human partiality and reveal divine will in distributing territory among the tribes. Proverbs 16:33 states the underlying theology explicitly: "the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." The same divinatory logic governs the Urim and Thummim of the priestly breastpiece (Exodus 28:30; 1 Samuel 14:41-42, where the Septuagint preserves a fuller text naming them), the detection of Achan by lot in Joshua 7:14-18, the selection of Saul as king in 1 Samuel 10:20-21, and the early Christians' choice of Matthias in Acts 1:26. Milgrom's JPS Numbers commentary and Nelson's Joshua volume both classify lot-casting as a divinatory ritual; Lindblom's foundational study treats it as a recognized mode of oracular inquiry. None of these is a wager: there is no risk of loss, no stake, no pursuit of gain — the defining features of gambling are absent.

The harmonization, then, dissolves the SAB's contradiction by correcting its categories rather than by special pleading. Proverbs 23:4 is not about gambling, and lot-casting in Numbers and Joshua is sortition for divinely-guided decision-making, not gaming. There is a genuine canonical silence on gambling as a modern phenomenon, since the practice in the relevant sense did not exist in the authors' world; whatever inferences one draws (perhaps from the warnings against laziness and the love of money in 1 Timothy 6:9-10) are extrapolations, not direct teaching.

A more interesting tension lurks nearby, and it is worth flagging because it is real where the SAB's is not. The soldiers who cast lots for Jesus' garments at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34; John 19:23-24, presented as fulfilling Psalm 22:18) perform the identical procedure that Numbers and Joshua treat as divinely commanded — yet here it is narrated as a callous act of Roman executioners dividing a victim's clothing. The act of casting lots thus carries opposite moral valences depending on who performs it and why, which suggests the biblical evaluation of the practice is situational rather than principled. That is a genuine wrinkle, but it concerns the moral status of lot-casting, not gambling, and so falls outside what the SAB actually asks.

Verdict: overstated. The specific contradiction rests on a non-gambling prooftext (Proverbs 23:4) and a misidentification of divinatory sortition as wagering; a real but adjacent tension exists over whether lot-casting is sacred or impious depending on context.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Category error: Proverbs 23:4 condemns the wearying pursuit of wealth, not gambling, which it never names; and the goral of Numbers/Joshua is a divinatory instrument for disclosing Yahweh's will (cf. Proverbs 16:33; Urim and Thummim), lacking the stake, risk, and gain that define gambling. The two answer-sets address different things, so the contradiction dissolves once the categories are corrected.

entries.question: Does God want some to go to hell?
entries.books_in_tension: Proverbs, John, Romans, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Peter
entries.summary: 1 Timothy 2:3-4 and 2 Peter 3:9 say God wants every human saved; Proverbs 16:4, John 12:40, Romans 9:18-22, and 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12 portray a deity who creates the wicked for the day of evil, hardens hearts to prevent repentance, prepares vessels of wrath, and sends strong delusion so that the damned will be damned. The two strands of texts presuppose flatly different doctrines of the divine will.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction the Calvinist-Arminian fight has tried to paper over for five hundred years, and the fact that the fight is still going tells you the texts genuinely point in opposite directions. The pastoral and 2 Peter say what they say: God 'wills all men to be saved' (pantas anthropous thelei sothenai, 1 Tim 2:4), and the Lord is 'not willing that any should perish' (me boulomenos tinas apolesthai, 2 Pet 3:9). I. Howard Marshall in the ICC Pastoral Epistles reads this as a deliberate anti-elitist polemic against any incipient Christian gnosticism that wanted to restrict salvation to an elect — a universal-salvific-will is the point of the passage.

Then you turn to Romans 9. Doug Moo in the NICNT Romans and Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB volume both grant that Paul is constructing a hard-doctrine-of-divine-sovereignty argument: God 'has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens' (Rom 9:18), and the 'vessels of wrath prepared for destruction' language (9:22) is the apostle's deliberate invocation of potter-and-clay sovereignty from Jeremiah and Isaiah. James Dunn in the WBC Romans 9-16 treats the chapter as Paul's most uncompromising statement of unconditional election. John 12:40 explicitly cites Isaiah 6:10 — God blinded their eyes so they would not turn and be healed. That's a divine intention to prevent conversion. C. K. Barrett's Gospel According to St. John commentary doesn't flinch: the evangelist means what he wrote.

The apologist harmonization runs through a distinction between God's 'revealed will' (he commands repentance, wants all saved) and his 'decretive will' (he ordains who actually gets saved). Wayne Grudem and Norman Geisler both run this play, and within a tight systematic-theology frame it's internally consistent. But notice what the move costs: you have to say that when 1 Timothy says God 'wills all to be saved,' the word 'wills' (thelei) means something different from when Romans 9 says God 'has mercy on whom he wills' (hon thelei eleei). Same Greek verb, same author's tradition, opposite force. That is post-hoc rationalization with the receipts of post-hoc rationalization.

The more honest reading is the one the critical scholars have been giving for a century: the pastoral and 2 Peter belong to a late-NT universalizing strand reacting against sectarian exclusivism, while Paul and Johannine apocalyptic preserve an older predestinarian instinct rooted in Second-Temple Jewish determinism. Different authors, different communities, different theologies. The Bible doesn't have a unified doctrine of God's saving will. That is of course a critical judgment on the evidence, but the textual variation is not a translation artifact.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is the contradiction over which the Calvinist–Arminian dispute has run for five centuries, and the persistence of the dispute is itself evidence that the texts pull in opposite directions. One stream affirms a universal salvific will in unambiguous terms. 1 Timothy 2:4 says God "wills all people to be saved" — pantas anthrōpous thelei sōthēnai — and 2 Peter 3:9 says the Lord is "not willing that any should perish" — mē boulomenos tinas apolesthai. I. Howard Marshall reads the pastoral statement as deliberate anti-elitist polemic against an incipient restriction of salvation to an elect circle; the universality of God's saving intent is the very point of the passage. Richard Bauckham reads 2 Peter 3:9 as a reworking of the delay-of-the-parousia problem in which God's patience is explained precisely by his desire for universal repentance.

The opposing stream is equally explicit and considerably harder. Romans 9 is Paul's most uncompromising statement of unconditional sovereignty: God "has mercy on whom he wills (hon thelei eleei), and whom he wills he hardens" (9:18), and the "vessels of wrath fitted for destruction" (9:22) deploy the potter-and-clay imagery Paul draws from Jeremiah 18 and Isaiah 29:16; 45:9. Both Douglas Moo and Joseph Fitzmyer grant that the argument is a hard doctrine of divine prerogative, and James Dunn treats the chapter as Paul's most absolute assertion of election. John 12:40 quotes Isaiah 6:10 to explain unbelief: God "has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see... and turn, and I heal them." Raymond Brown and C. K. Barrett both decline to soften it; the Fourth Evangelist presents divine action that prevents conversion. Proverbs 16:4 ("YHWH made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble") and 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12 (God "sends them a strong delusion... that they all might be condemned") complete the pattern of a deity who ordains the ruin of the reprobate.

The standard harmonization is the dogmatic distinction between God's revealed (preceptive) will and his decretive (secret) will: God genuinely commands repentance and in that sense wills all saved, while in his hidden decree he ordains who is actually saved. Wayne Grudem articulates the distinction carefully, and Norman Geisler deploys a related framework. Within a closed systematic-theological system the move is internally consistent, and it deserves to be stated at full strength rather than caricatured. The exegetical cost, however, is steep. It requires that thelō mean "sincere universal desire" in 1 Timothy 2:4 and "effectual sovereign choice" in Romans 9:18 — the same verb, in the same Pauline tradition, carrying opposite force, with the disambiguation supplied not by the texts but by the system that needs them harmonized. That is the signature of post-hoc rationalization.

The critical reading locates the divergence historically. As E. P. Sanders showed, Second-Temple Judaism held divine sovereignty and human accountability in unintegrated tension, and the Qumran determinism of texts like the Treatise on the Two Spirits supplied a predestinarian matrix Paul partly inherited. The pastorals and 2 Peter belong to a later, universalizing stratum reacting against sectarian exclusivism, while Paul and Johannine apocalyptic preserve the older deterministic instinct. Different authors, communities, and theologies produced statements that a single doctrine of the divine will cannot smoothly contain. Verdict: a real and disputed contradiction; harmonizable only by importing a will-distinction the texts themselves do not supply.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Reformed systematic theology resolves the tension by distinguishing God's revealed/preceptive will (he commands repentance and wills all saved) from his decretive/secret will (he ordains who is actually saved); the resolution is internally coherent within that dogmatic frame but is contested because it must assign different force to thelō across texts from the same tradition and is widely judged exegetically post-hoc.

entries.question: Is it good to be happy?
entries.summary: Proverbs 17:22 and Ecclesiastes 8:15 commend merriment as medicinal and as the best thing humans can do under the sun. Ecclesiastes 7:3-4 and Luke 6:25 reverse the valuation — sorrow is better than laughter, the wise heart is in the house of mourning, and woe to those who laugh now. Even Qohelet contradicts himself on this question, and Luke's Jesus piles on from the other direction.
entries.commentary:
The most interesting feature of this contradiction is that it lives inside a single biblical book. Qohelet says both. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes volume documents at length how the book oscillates between carpe diem affirmations (2:24, 3:12-13, 5:18, 8:15, 9:7-10) and meditations on the moral seriousness of grief (1:18, 4:1-3, 7:1-4). Seow reads the tension as Qohelet's deliberate dialectic: pleasure is the best thing available, and pleasure is hollow. Both claims, simultaneously, by design. Tremper Longman in the NICOT volume gets to the same place by a different route, calling Qohelet's voice a 'frame narrator' wrestling with two theological postures the wisdom tradition couldn't synthesize.

Then there's Proverbs 17:22, which is the wisdom tradition in its sunniest mood. Michael Fox in the AYB Proverbs reads the lev sameah — merry heart — as proto-psychosomatic medicine: cheerful disposition produces physical wellbeing. It's the kind of claim you find in Egyptian Instruction literature and in much later Greek medical writing. The book of Proverbs likes happiness.

Luke 6:25 is operating in an apocalyptic-prophetic register that does not. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke volume reads the woes-and-beatitudes structure as classic prophetic reversal-language: those who laugh now will mourn later precisely because the present age is upside-down. François Bovon in the Hermeneia Luke 1 volume frames the woe as deliberate inversion of Hellenistic eudaimonia — Jesus is attacking the comfortable presupposition that present happiness is a sign of divine favor. The verse isn't poetry. It's eschatological reversal: enjoy your laughter now, the kingdom is coming and the ledger is going to be balanced.

The apologist harmonization runs through 'different kinds of happiness' — worldly mirth vs. spiritual joy, frivolous laughter vs. mature contentment. Apologetic commentators have run this distinction hard. But Qohelet uses the same Hebrew root (smḥ) for the merriment he praises and the laughter he mocks; Luke uses the same Greek root (gelao) for the laughter that will become mourning. The vocabulary isn't doing the work the harmonization needs it to do. You're left with a wisdom tradition that says be happy, a wisdom tradition that says don't be too happy, and a Jesus tradition that says happiness now is a downpayment on woe. The Bible doesn't speak with one voice on whether human happiness is good.

commentary_out.commentary:
The sharpest feature of this contradiction is that one biblical book holds both poles at once. Qohelet commends mirth and disparages it within the same composition. Choon-Leong Seow catalogues the carpe-diem refrains scattered through Ecclesiastes — 2:24-26; 3:12-13; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10 — in which eating, drinking, and enjoyment are repeatedly named the best a human can do "under the sun," and sets them against the meditations on the gravity of grief in 1:18; 4:1-3; and 7:1-4. Ecclesiastes 8:15 "commends enjoyment" (wəšibbaḥtî ʾănî ʾet-haśśimḥâ) as the supreme available good; Ecclesiastes 7:3-4 declares sorrow better than laughter and locates the wise heart "in the house of mourning." Seow reads the oscillation as a deliberate dialectic rather than editorial confusion: pleasure is simultaneously the best thing on offer and ultimately hevel, vapor. Tremper Longman reaches a similar conclusion through the frame-narrator hypothesis, in which the book stages two theological postures the wisdom tradition could not synthesize. Either way, the affirmation and the negation of happiness stand side by side by authorial design.

Proverbs 17:22 represents the tradition in its sunniest register: lēb śāmēaḥ yêṭib gēhâ — "a joyful heart is good medicine." Michael Fox reads the line as proto-psychosomatic observation, the kind of claim paralleled in Egyptian Instruction literature and later Greek medical writing: cheerfulness produces physical wellbeing. Proverbs, on this verse, simply likes happiness and treats it as health-giving.

Luke 6:25 operates in an apocalyptic-prophetic register that does not. Joseph Fitzmyer reads the woes paired with the beatitudes (Luke 6:20-26) as classic prophetic reversal language: ouai... hoi gelōntes nyn, hoti penthēsete kai klausete — "woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep." François Bovon frames the woe as a deliberate inversion of Hellenistic eudaimonia, an attack on the comfortable assumption that present contentment signals divine favor. The verse is not aesthetic counsel about moderation; it is eschatological reversal — present laughter is a debt that the coming kingdom will call in.

The standard harmonization distinguishes kinds of happiness: worldly mirth versus spiritual joy, frivolous laughter versus mature contentment. The lexical evidence resists the move. Qohelet uses the same root, śmḥ, for the merriment he commends in 8:15 and the laughter he disparages in 7:3-4 and 2:2 ("of laughter I said, it is mad"); Luke uses the same verb, gelaō, for the blessed laughter promised in 6:21 and the condemned laughter of 6:25. The vocabulary does not partition itself into a sanctioned and an unsanctioned species of joy; the same words carry the positive and negative valuations, so the distinction must be imported rather than read out. James Crenshaw's analysis of Qohelet underscores that the book's tensions are not resolved by such glosses but are constitutive of its theology of contingency.

What remains is three positions that do not reconcile: a wisdom tradition that prescribes happiness as medicine (Proverbs), a wisdom voice that both commends and indicts it (Qohelet), and a Jesus tradition that treats present happiness as a down payment on future woe (Luke). The contradiction is real, and in Ecclesiastes it is internal to a single book. Verdict: genuine contradiction, partly intra-textual.

issues.problem: The commentary's central lexical claim that Luke 6:21 and 6:25 use 'the same verb gelaō' for blessed and condemned laughter is only partly accurate. Luke 6:21 reads gelasete ('you will laugh') and 6:25 reads hoi gelōntes nyn... and the woe pair uses gelaō in both, so that part holds. However the parallel between the blessed laughter (future, eschatological reward in 6:21) and condemned present laughter (6:25) is precisely a temporal/eschatological distinction (laughter NOW vs. laughter THEN), which somewhat undercuts the claim that 'the same words carry positive and negative valuations' without distinction — Luke himself supplies a temporal qualifier (nyn, 'now'). The argument that vocabulary alone defeats the harmonization is therefore slightly overstated for the Luke half.
issues.correction: Acknowledge that in Luke the valuation hinges on the explicit temporal marker nyn ('now') — present laughter vs. future/eschatological laughter — so Luke himself distinguishes the two by time, even if using the same verb; the lexical-identity point is stronger for Qohelet's śmḥ than for Luke's gelaō.

entries.question: Does hell exist?
entries.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, Joshua, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Daniel, Obadiah, Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, Hebrews, James, 1 John, Jude, Revelation
entries.summary: The Bible offers four mutually incompatible afterlife schemes. The apocalyptic strand (Daniel 12, Matthew, Mark, Luke, 2 Thessalonians, Hebrews, Jude, Revelation) describes eternal conscious torment. The annihilationist strand (Psalms, Proverbs, Obadiah, Romans, Galatians, Philippians, James) describes the wicked being destroyed, perishing, and ceasing to exist. The universalist strand (1 Cor 15:22, 1 Tim 4:10, 1 John 2:2) has all humans made alive in Christ. And the Sheol-only strand (Job, Psalms, Qohelet, Isaiah 38) has everyone going to the same silent dust regardless of moral state. Critical scholarship reads this as four overlapping historical layers, not one coherent doctrine.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that makes the most theological mileage, because the four positions are each defended by living religious communities — eternal-conscious-torment by traditional evangelicals and Catholics, annihilationism by conditionalists like Edward Fudge and a growing slice of evangelical scholars, universalism by figures like David Bentley Hart and Robin Parry, and the Sheol-only / no-afterlife reading by critical scholarship of the Hebrew Bible. Each side has the receipts because each set of texts genuinely says what those communities claim it says.

Start with the no-afterlife strand, because the apologist playbook page one is to pretend it doesn't exist. Job 7:9, Job 14:10-14, Ecclesiastes 3:19-21, Ecclesiastes 9:5-6, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 88:5, Psalm 115:17, Isaiah 38:18 — these are not isolated outliers. James Crenshaw in the OTL Ecclesiastes and Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes both treat Qohelet's denial of post-mortem reward as the book's foundational anthropology. Jon Levenson in *Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel* documents how the pre-exilic and early post-exilic Hebrew Bible has no developed afterlife — Sheol is just the grave-shadow, the same for everyone. The apocalyptic resurrection of Daniel 12 is, on Levenson's reading, a late innovation responding to Maccabean martyrdom. John Collins in the Hermeneia Daniel commentary nails the date: Daniel 12:2 is the first unambiguous biblical reference to differential post-mortem destinies, and it's from the 160s BCE.

Then the eternal-torment strand. Dale Allison in the ICC Matthew documents at length how Matthean apocalyptic deploys Gehenna imagery from Isaiah 66:24 and 1 Enoch to portray actual unending punishment. Joel Marcus on Mark 9:43-48 in the AYB doesn't soften the imagery — the worm that doesn't die and the fire that isn't quenched are deliberately permanent. David Aune in the WBC Revelation 17-22 reads the lake-of-fire torment 'forever and ever' (eis tous aionas ton aionon) as as strong as Greek can make the duration claim. So the apocalyptic strand is real, and it's not the sole property of medieval imagination.

Then the annihilationist strand, which uses the verbs the eternal-torment crowd would prefer to soften. Apollymi (perish), phtheiro (destroy), olethros (destruction) — these are destruction-words, and the texts say what they say. Edward Fudge in *The Fire That Consumes* and Glenn Peoples have made the conditionalist case from a confessionally evangelical position; you don't have to go to atheists for it. Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, not eternal torment. 2 Thessalonians 1:9 says olethron aionion — eternal destruction — which conditionalists read as 'permanent destruction' (the result is eternal, not the process). Then the universalist strand — 1 Cor 15:22's 'in Adam all die, in Christ all shall be made alive' (pantes zōopoiēthēsontai) — has Origen and the Cappadocians arguing apokatastasis is the actual New Testament eschatology. David Bentley Hart's *That All Shall Be Saved* re-litigates the Greek and makes the case that eternal torment isn't even in the Pauline letters.

The harmonization attempts boil down to assigning different texts to different vocabularies — Sheol means the grave but not the soul, perishing means losing relationship not existence, universalist verses are about potential not actual scope. Each move can be defended in isolation, but the combined harmonization requires four different translation conventions enforced selectively. The honest critical reading is the developmental one: the Hebrew Bible mostly has no afterlife, the late Second Temple period imports differential post-mortem destinies from Persian and Hellenistic sources, early Christianity carries forward the apocalyptic version, and the universalist and annihilationist strands are minority readings that survived inside the canon. The Bible doesn't teach a single doctrine of hell. Take your pick — which is exactly what every Christian tradition has been doing for two thousand years.

commentary_out.commentary:
This contradiction generates so much theological friction because all four positions are defended today by living communities that read their proof-texts correctly. Eternal conscious torment is held by traditional evangelicals and Catholics; annihilationism (conditional immortality) by conditionalists such as Edward Fudge and a growing slice of evangelical scholars; universalism by figures like David Bentley Hart and Robin Parry; and the no-afterlife / Sheol-only reading is simply what critical scholarship finds in the bulk of the Hebrew Bible. Each side has the receipts because each cluster of texts genuinely says what those communities claim.

Begin with the no-afterlife strand, since the apologetic playbook's first move is to act as if it isn't there. Job 7:9, Job 14:10-14, Ecclesiastes 3:19-21, Ecclesiastes 9:5-6, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 88:5, Psalm 115:17, and Isaiah 38:18 are not stray outliers. James Crenshaw (OTL Ecclesiastes) and Choon-Leong Seow (AB Ecclesiastes) both treat Qohelet's denial of any post-mortem reward as the book's foundational anthropology — the dead "know nothing," the same fate befalls human and beast. Jon Levenson, in *Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel*, documents how the pre-exilic and early post-exilic Hebrew Bible has no developed afterlife: *Sheol* is the undifferentiated grave-shadow, identical for righteous and wicked. Philip Johnston's *Shades of Sheol* reaches the same conclusion through close lexical work. The decisive datum is chronological: John Collins, in the Hermeneia Daniel, establishes that Daniel 12:2 — "many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life, some to everlasting contempt" — is the first unambiguous biblical reference to differential post-mortem destinies, composed in the 160s BCE in direct response to the Maccabean martyrdoms, when the problem of righteous sufferers who died unvindicated forced the innovation. The likely catalysts were Persian (Zoroastrian dualistic eschatology) and Hellenistic, absorbed across the late Second Temple period.

The eternal-torment strand is equally real. Dale Allison (ICC Matthew) shows how Matthean apocalyptic deploys Gehenna imagery drawn from Isaiah 66:24 and 1 Enoch to portray unending punishment. Joel Marcus, on Mark 9:43-48, declines to soften the imagery: the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched are quoted from Isaiah precisely for their permanence. Aune reads Revelation's lake-of-fire torment *eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn* ("forever and ever") as as strong a duration claim as Greek can make. So the apocalyptic hell is not a medieval invention.

The annihilationist strand turns on the verbs the torment reading would prefer to soften. *Apollymi* (perish), *phtheirō*/*phthora* (destroy, corruption), and *olethros* (destruction) are destruction-words. Romans 6:23 sets the wage of sin as *thanatos* (death), not torment; Philippians 3:19 names the enemies' *telos* as *apōleia*; 2 Thessalonians 1:9 has *olethron aiōnion*, which conditionalists construe as a destruction whose *result* is permanent, not a destroying that never finishes. Fudge's *The Fire That Consumes* and Glenn Peoples make this case from within evangelical confession, not from skepticism. The universalist strand rests on texts like 1 Cor 15:22 — "as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive" (*pantes zōopoiēthēsontai*) — 1 Tim 4:10 (God "the Savior of all"), and 1 John 2:2 (propitiation "for the whole world"). Origen and the Cappadocians argued *apokatastasis* from precisely these; Hart's *That All Shall Be Saved* re-litigates the Greek, contending that the *aiōnios* word-group denotes the age to come rather than infinite duration, so that "eternal torment" is not even securely present in Paul.

The harmonizations all reduce to assigning different texts to different vocabularies enforced selectively: *Sheol* means the body's grave but not the conscious soul; "perish" means loss of relationship, not loss of existence; the universalist verses describe potential scope, not actual outcome; *aiōnios* means "eternal" for heaven but "resultant" for destruction. Each move is defensible in isolation; the trouble is that a single coherent doctrine requires all four conventions at once, applied inconsistently to keep one preferred picture standing. The honest critical reading is developmental: the Hebrew Bible mostly has no afterlife; the late Second Temple period imports differential destinies from Persian and Hellenistic sources; early Christianity carries the apocalyptic version forward while the annihilationist and universalist strands survive as canonical minority reports. Verdict: genuine contradiction — the canon preserves at least four incompatible eschatologies rather than one.

entries.question: Is money good or bad?
entries.summary: Ecclesiastes 10:19 says money answers all things — every problem in life has a financial solution. 1 Timothy 6:10 says the love of money is the root of all evil. One is wisdom-tradition pragmatism about wealth's utility; the other is Hellenistic-Jewish moralism about wealth's spiritual danger.
entries.commentary:
The apologist move on this one is to point out that 1 Timothy 6:10 doesn't say money is the root of all evil — it says philargyria, the love of money, is. That's correct as far as it goes. The KJV's 'love of money is the root of all evil' is technically accurate, even if the indefinite-article rendering 'a root of all kinds of evils' (NRSV, NA28) softens it slightly. Luke Timothy Johnson in the AB Pastoral Epistles documents that philargyria was a stock Hellenistic moralist topos — the same Greek term shows up in Diogenes Laertius and Polybius as a fundamental vice. So 1 Timothy 6:10 is doing standard Greco-Roman ethics: greed corrupts.

But Ecclesiastes 10:19 isn't saying anything about greed. Qohelet says ha-kesef yaaneh et ha-kol — silver answers all. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes reads this as Qohelet's characteristic dark realism: money is the universal solvent of human problems, full stop. Not 'money has its dangers but useful in moderation' — money answers everything. Tremper Longman in the NICOT volume notes that Qohelet's claim is being made within a book that is otherwise quite ready to denounce the hoarding of wealth (5:10-17), so 10:19 is a deliberately unsentimental observation about how money actually functions in the social world.

The harmonization usually goes through carve-outs: Ecclesiastes is describing how things are; 1 Timothy is describing how things should be. That's a fair reading and it does relieve some of the tension. But notice what it concedes — Qohelet is teaching that the actual, real-world function of wealth is to answer all problems, and the Christian moral tradition is telling you to repudiate that exact attitude. The Bible contains both the cynical pragmatism and the moralistic warning. Whether that counts as 'contradiction' or 'tension within a multi-voiced canon' depends on how charitable you want to be about canonical pluralism. The critical reading is that the wisdom-pragmatist strand and the apocalyptic-moralist strand have always pulled in opposite directions on wealth, and the Bible never resolves the fight — it just lets both voices speak.

answers.answer_explanation: For the love of money is the root of all evil. 1 Timothy 6:10

commentary_out.commentary:
The first apologetic correction here is both fair and necessary: 1 Timothy 6:10 does not say money is the root of all evil but that the *love* of money — *philargyria* — is. The KJV's "the love of money is the root of all evil" is lexically accurate; the critical text and most modern versions (NRSV, NA28) render the article-less Greek as "a root of all kinds of evils" (*riza … pantōn tōn kakōn*), which is grammatically the stronger reading and softens the universal sweep. Luke Timothy Johnson, in the Anchor Bible Pastoral Epistles, documents that *philargyria* was a stock topos of Hellenistic moral philosophy: the noun and its cognates recur in Diogenes Laertius, Polybius, and the diatribe tradition as a paradigmatic vice, often paired with warnings that greed breeds every other transgression. Abraham Malherbe's survey of the Hellenistic moralists and the New Testament places the Pastorals squarely in that ethical idiom. I. Howard Marshall's ICC commentary concurs: 1 Tim 6:10 is conventional Greco-Roman ethics baptized into a Christian paraenesis — greed corrupts, contentment is gain.

Ecclesiastes 10:19, however, is not talking about greed at all, and that is what makes the tension real rather than verbal. Qohelet writes *ha-kesef yaʿaneh ʾet ha-kol* — "silver/money answers everything." Choon-Leong Seow, in the Anchor Bible Ecclesiastes, reads this as Qohelet's characteristic unsentimental realism: money is the universal solvent of human problems, stated without moral hedging. The verb *ʿanah* ("answer, respond, meet the need of") frames money as the thing that responds to every demand. Tremper Longman, in the NICOT, and James Crenshaw, in the OTL, both note the bite of this: it appears in a book that elsewhere denounces the hoarding of wealth in unsparing terms (5:10-17 — "he who loves money will not be satisfied with money"; riches kept by their owner to his hurt; the rich man's full belly that will not let him sleep). So Qohelet himself holds the descriptive observation (money fixes things) and a warning against money-lust in tension within one book — which is precisely why 10:19 cannot be read as naïve endorsement, but neither can it be read as a moral caution. It is a flat observation about how wealth functions in the social world.

The usual harmonization runs through the descriptive/prescriptive distinction: Ecclesiastes describes how things are (money does, in fact, answer many problems), while 1 Timothy prescribes how one should be disposed (do not love it). This is a genuinely fair reading and it relieves much of the surface tension; the two verses are not strictly affirming and denying the same proposition, since one concerns money's utility and the other concerns the affective orientation of greed. But it is worth naming what the harmonization concedes. Qohelet is teaching, as wisdom, that the real-world function of wealth is to answer all things — a claim the Christian moralist tradition is precisely warning the reader not to internalize, because to believe that money answers everything is the cognitive engine of *philargyria*. The descriptive observation and the prescriptive warning are not formal contradictories, but they pull in opposite directions and reflect two different evaluative postures toward wealth that the canon never reconciles: a wisdom-pragmatist realism that treats money as the universal answer, and a Hellenistic-Jewish moralism that treats love of it as the universal corrupter. Whether one labels this "contradiction" or "tension within a multi-voiced canon" depends on how strictly one defines the terms. Verdict: partially harmonizable — no formal logical contradiction once the descriptive/prescriptive and lexical distinctions are honored, but a genuine and unresolved clash of evaluative outlooks on wealth.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The two verses are not strict contradictories: 1 Tim 6:10 condemns philargyria (the disposition of greed), not money itself, while Eccl 10:19 makes a descriptive observation about money's social utility. The descriptive/prescriptive distinction plus the lexical point ('a root of all kinds of evils', love of money) dissolves the formal contradiction, though a real clash of evaluative postures toward wealth remains.

entries.question: Will the Messiah be a descendant of David?
entries.summary: Isaiah 11:1 and Jeremiah 23:5-6 promise a Davidic messiah — a Branch from David's line who will reign as king. In Mark 12:35-37, Jesus quotes Psalm 110 and argues that the Messiah cannot be David's son because David himself calls him 'Lord.' The Synoptic Jesus is denying the very Davidic-descent expectation that the prophets and the genealogies of Matthew and Luke spent so much energy establishing.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the New Testament is genuinely at war with itself. Matthew 1 and Luke 3 supply elaborate (and mutually incompatible) genealogies establishing Jesus's Davidic descent. Romans 1:3 calls Jesus 'descended from David according to the flesh.' Revelation 5:5 calls him 'the Root of David.' The Davidic-messiah expectation in Second Temple Judaism is documented exhaustively — John Collins in *The Scepter and the Star* shows that the Psalms of Solomon 17, the Qumran 4Q174 Florilegium, and the Sibylline Oracles all expected an actual biological descendant of David.

Then Mark 12:35-37 has Jesus standing in the temple and asking — pos legousin hoi grammateis hoti ho christos huios estin Dauid — 'how do the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?' He quotes Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1): the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. If David calls him Lord, Jesus argues, how is he his son? The rhetorical force of the question implies the messiah is not David's son — he's David's Lord, someone above David in the cosmic hierarchy. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark 8-16 reads this pericope as a deliberate problematizing of the Davidic-descent tradition, possibly reflecting an early christology in which the post-resurrection enthronement (Psalm 110) mattered more than biological lineage. Adela Yarbro Collins in the Hermeneia Mark gets to the same conclusion: the Markan Jesus is challenging the messianic paradigm the scribes assumed.

The apologist harmonization usually runs through two paths. Path one: Jesus isn't denying he's David's son; he's pointing out that 'son of David' isn't sufficient — he's also more than that, a divine figure exalted above David. Craig Evans in the WBC Mark 8:27-16:20 makes this case at length. Path two: the genealogies in Matthew and Luke establish legal descent through Joseph, while the Markan pericope is pointing toward a higher Christology that's compatible with that legal descent. Both paths have textual support, and they're not absurd readings.

But here's the problem. The Markan question is rhetorical, and the rhetorical force depends on the conclusion that the Messiah is not the son of David. If Jesus is okay with also being David's son, the question doesn't work — David would just be addressing his future descendant in advance, and there's no scandal in calling one's distant scion 'Lord.' The Markan logic only sings if the Davidic-descent expectation is being challenged. And then the Pauline 'descended from David according to the flesh' and the Matthean and Lukan genealogies are doing the opposite work. The simplest critical reading is that the early Christian movement contained both an exaltation-Christology that didn't need Davidic biology and a Davidic-Messiah Christology that did, and the canon preserves both without reconciling them. Take your pick — Jesus the Davidic king, or Jesus the pre-existent Lord whose David-descent the Markan polemic was already trying to relativize.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the New Testament is at war with itself. Matthew 1 and Luke 3 supply elaborate — and mutually incompatible — genealogies establishing Jesus's Davidic descent (Raymond Brown's Birth of the Messiah documents both the discrepancies between the two lists and their shared insistence on Davidic lineage through Joseph). Romans 1:3, in what most scholars regard as a pre-Pauline confessional formula Paul is quoting, calls Jesus 'descended from David according to the flesh' (genomenou ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka); Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Romans treats this as traditional material Paul inherited, which makes the Davidic-descent claim demonstrably early. Revelation 5:5 calls him 'the Root of David.' The Davidic-messiah expectation in Second Temple Judaism is documented exhaustively: John Collins in The Scepter and the Star shows that Psalms of Solomon 17, the Qumran 4Q174 (Florilegium) reading of 2 Samuel 7, and related texts expected an actual biological 'son of David' who would reign as king.

Then Mark 12:35-37 has Jesus in the temple asking, pōs legousin hoi grammateis hoti ho christos huios estin Dauid — 'how do the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?' He quotes Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1): eipen ho kyrios tō kyriō mou, 'the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.' If David, speaking 'by the Holy Spirit,' calls the Messiah 'Lord,' how is the Messiah his son? Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark 8-16 reads the pericope as a deliberate problematizing of the Davidic-descent tradition, plausibly reflecting an early exaltation Christology in which the post-resurrection enthronement at God's right hand (the point of citing Ps 110) mattered more than biological lineage. Adela Yarbro Collins in the Hermeneia Mark reaches the same conclusion: the Markan Jesus challenges the messianic paradigm the scribes assumed.

The apologetic harmonization runs two ways, and both deserve a fair hearing. Path one (Craig Evans, WBC Mark): Jesus is not denying Davidic sonship but showing it insufficient — he is David's son and more, a figure exalted above David, so the riddle exposes the scribes' inadequate Christology rather than refuting the genealogies. Path two: the Matthean and Lukan genealogies establish legal descent through Joseph, which is compatible with a higher Christology pointing beyond mere lineage. Neither reading is absurd, and Evans's case has real textual purchase.

But the harmonization runs aground on the rhetorical mechanics of the question. A rhetorical question carries force only if its implied answer is decisive. If the Markan Jesus were content to be also David's son, the question collapses: a king addressing his own future descendant as 'Lord' is no scandal, because nothing prevents one's distant scion from being one's superior — that is precisely what an exalted-descendant Christology would say. The puzzle only bites if 'son of David' and 'David's Lord' are being treated as incompatible, i.e., if Davidic descent is being relativized or denied. Yet Romans 1:3, the genealogies, and Revelation 5:5 affirm exactly the descent Mark's logic strains against. The most economical critical reading is that the early Jesus movement contained both an exaltation Christology that did not require Davidic biology and a Davidic-messiah Christology that did, and the canon preserves both without reconciling them. Verdict: a genuine internal contradiction reflecting two competing early Christologies.

entries.question: On what did Jesus ride into Jerusalem?
entries.summary: Matthew 21:5-7 has Jesus ride into Jerusalem on two animals — a donkey and a colt — with the disciples laying garments on both and Jesus sitting on 'them.' Mark 11:7 and Luke 19:35 have him ride a single colt. John 12:14 has him on a 'young donkey.' Matthew's two-animal version is unique among the four gospels.
entries.commentary:
Here's the thing — this is one of the cleanest examples of Matthew clumsily literalizing an Old Testament prophecy. Zechariah 9:9 reads (NRSV): 'humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.' That's standard Hebrew synonymous parallelism — one animal, described twice for poetic emphasis (cf. Meyers and Meyers, *Zechariah 9-14* AB 25C). Mark, Luke, and John all read it that way: one animal.

Matthew didn't. Matthew 21:7 says they brought *tēn onon kai ton pōlon* ('the donkey and the colt'), put garments *ep' autōn* ('on them'), and Jesus sat *epanō autōn* ('upon them'). Whether Matthew imagined Jesus straddling both animals at once or shifting between them is a problem the text creates and doesn't solve.

The apologist harmonization, defended by Blomberg in *The Historical Reliability of the Gospels* and by Carson in the Expositor's commentary, runs two ways. Path one: 'them' refers to the garments, not the animals. That's syntactically possible but awkward — the immediate antecedent is the animals, not the garments. Path two: the mother donkey was led alongside and Jesus actually rode the colt; Matthew just got vague. That requires reading Mark/Luke/John back into Matthew, which is exactly the maneuver historical critics object to.

The consensus reading among critical scholars — Davies and Allison's three-volume ICC, Luz's Hermeneia, Nolland's NIGTC — is that Matthew misread the Hebrew parallelism, took 'a donkey and a colt' as two animals, and adjusted his Markan source to fit. It's not a contradiction in the sense that the same event is described two incompatible ways; it's a contradiction in the sense that Matthew's version has Jesus doing something physically awkward to satisfy a prophecy that didn't require it.

Verdict: Mark/Luke/John have one animal. Matthew has two. The harmonization either tortures the syntax or admits Matthew was vague in a way that conveniently looks like Mark/Luke/John.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest demonstrable cases of Matthew literalizing an Old Testament prophecy at the cost of narrative plausibility. The hinge is Zechariah 9:9, which the LXX and Hebrew render as a single rider: 'humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey' (*ʿānî wĕrōkēb ʿal-ḥămôr wĕʿal-ʿayir ben-ʾătōnôt*). This is textbook Hebrew synonymous parallelism — one animal named twice for poetic intensification, the second colon restating the first. Meyers and Meyers in the Anchor Bible Zechariah volume read it that way without hesitation, as does virtually all Hebrew scholarship. Mark 11:7, Luke 19:35, and John 12:14 each have a single animal, a *pōlos* (colt) on which Jesus sits; John even quotes Zechariah and pluralizes nothing.

Matthew alone produces two animals. Matthew 21:2 has Jesus send for 'a donkey tied, and a colt with her' (*onon dedemenēn kai pōlon met' autēs*); 21:5 quotes Zechariah with the Greek *kai* read as straightforwardly additive ('on a donkey, *and* on a colt') rather than as parallelism; and 21:7 then reports that the disciples 'brought the donkey and the colt (*tēn onon kai ton pōlon*), and put their cloaks on them (*ep' autōn*), and he sat on them (*epanō autōn*).' The two-animal reading is built into the entire pericope, not a slip in one verse.

The apologetic harmonization runs along two paths, and both are defended in their strongest form by Blomberg and by Carson in the Expositor's commentary. Path one: the final *autōn* ('on them') refers to the garments, not the animals — Jesus sat on the cloaks, which had been spread on both beasts. This is grammatically possible: *autōn* is a bare genitive plural and Greek allows some latitude in antecedent. But it is awkward, because the nearest and most natural antecedent of *epanō autōn* is the immediately preceding pair of animals, and the *ep' autōn* clause earlier in the same verse plainly does place the cloaks 'on them' (the animals). Path two: the mother donkey was simply led alongside for the colt's sake — an unbroken colt being calmer with its dam present — and Matthew, knowing two animals were involved, mentioned both while Jesus actually rode only the colt. This is the most plausible defense and cannot be strictly disproven; but it rescues Matthew only by importing Mark/Luke/John's single rider back into Matthew and treating Matthew's own *epanō autōn* as loose.

The decisive evidence is redaction-critical and lies in Matthew's demonstrable compositional habit. Working from Mark (Markan priority being the consensus solution to the Synoptic Problem), Matthew repeatedly doubles single figures in his source: Mark's one Gerasene demoniac becomes two (Matt 8:28 vs. Mark 5:2); Mark's one blind man at Jericho, Bartimaeus, becomes two (Matt 20:30 vs. Mark 10:46). Whatever the reason for this pattern, it shows Matthew is capable of numerical adjustment for his own purposes. In the triumphal entry the adjustment is driven by the formula-citation: Matthew has the strongest interest among the evangelists in showing Jesus fulfilling Scripture down to the detail, and here that interest led him to read Zechariah's parallel cola as two distinct animals and to stage the scene accordingly. Davies and Allison (ICC), Luz (Hermeneia), and Nolland (NIGTC) converge on this judgment.

This is therefore not a case of two narrators describing one event in mutually exclusive ways at the level of brute fact; it is a case of Matthew's account requiring Jesus to be associated with two animals in a way the other three Gospels and the Hebrew of Zechariah do not, generated by a misconstrual of poetic parallelism. The harmonizations do not eliminate the difficulty so much as relocate it: either the syntax of *epanō autōn* must be strained, or Matthew must be conceded to be vague in precisely the way that conveniently reconciles him with his sources — which concedes the redactional point.

Verdict: genuine compositional discrepancy — Matthew's two animals against the single colt of Mark, Luke, and John.

entries.question: How many generations from Jesus to Abraham?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:17 states explicitly: 14 generations from Abraham to David, 14 from David to the deportation, 14 from the deportation to Christ — 42 total. Count the actual names in Matthew 1:1-17 and you get 41. Matthew's stated arithmetic does not match Matthew's own list.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in the New Testament because it's Matthew vs. Matthew. The author asserts a numerical scheme (3 x 14 = 42) and then provides the list that doesn't add up.

Count the names: Abraham to David inclusive is 14 (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David). David to the deportation (Jeconiah) is 14 *if* you count David twice (David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jeconiah — that's 15 starting from David, or 14 starting from Solomon). The deportation to Christ is only 13 (Jeconiah, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph, Jesus — that's 14 if you count Jeconiah twice, or 13 if you don't).

The apologist harmonization, run by Carson in EBC and the standard evangelical introductions, is that David and Jeconiah are pivot figures counted in both their adjacent groups, which lets you get 14 + 14 + 14 with the same person doing double duty. That works mathematically but it's a manipulation — you're claiming 42 generations while only having 41 distinct individuals. If David and Jeconiah each count twice, the *generation count* from Abraham to Jesus is 41, not 42, because a person isn't two generations.

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison ICC, Luz Hermeneia, Brown *Birth of the Messiah*) is that Matthew himself knew the numbers were tight — the 3x14 scheme is built on the gematria of David's name (D-V-D = 4+6+4 = 14) — and he made the count work by manipulating his source. He may have dropped three Judahite kings (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah between Joram and Uzziah, cf. 1 Chr 3:11-12) precisely to hit his 14-14-14 target. The arithmetic problem is what's left over after the manipulation.

Verdict: Matthew claims 42, Matthew lists 41. The harmonization that counts David and Jeconiah twice produces 42 generation-slots but only 41 generations of human beings. The numerology is doing the work; the genealogy is paying the cost.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is a rare instance of an internal numerical tension that is Matthew against Matthew: the Evangelist asserts a scheme of three fourteens (1:17) and then supplies a list that, counted naively, yields forty-one distinct individuals rather than forty-two slots. The summary statement and the actual roster do not obviously cohere.

The organizing principle is not chronological but numerological. "Fourteen" is the gematria value of David's name in Hebrew: D-V-D (dalet-waw-dalet) = 4 + 6 + 4 = 14. Matthew, writing a Davidic-messianic Gospel that opens *biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou huiou Dauid* (1:1), structures the genealogy so that David's number governs all three epochs of Israel's story — patriarchs to king, king to exile, exile to Messiah. Davies-Allison, Luz, and Brown all regard the 3×14 as a deliberate mnemonic-theological device rather than a census, and most note that Matthew has pruned his source to hit the number: between Joram and Uzziah (1:8) he omits three reigning Judahite kings — Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah — who appear in the Chronicler's line (1 Chr 3:11-12). That omission is the clearest evidence that the count is engineered.

The counting itself is genuinely defensible once one grasps the design. From Abraham to David is fourteen with David as the fourteenth. From David (or Solomon) to the exile is fourteen. From the exile to Jesus is fourteen if Jechoniah is counted in this third panel. The standard evangelical harmonization, articulated by Carson, makes David and Jechoniah "pivot" figures, each belonging to two epochs — David closes group one and opens group two; the deportation generation closes group two and Jechoniah opens group three. This is not an ad hoc rescue: Matthew's own wording invites it, since each summary clause is bounded by an event (David, the deportation, Christ) and the boundary figures naturally sit on both sides. On this reading the arithmetic of the *clauses* is internally coherent.

What the harmonization concedes is the more interesting point. If David and Jechoniah are each counted twice to reach forty-two, then the number of distinct human generations from Abraham to Jesus is forty-one, not forty-two — a single person is not two generations. The text is best read as claiming forty-two named *positions* across an overlapping triadic scheme, not forty-two consecutive begettings. There is also a textual wrinkle: a number of witnesses and the surrounding tradition show confusion at 1:11 over whether Jehoiakim should stand between Josiah and Jechoniah, and some early scribes evidently tried to add a name to round the third group to a clean fourteen — evidence that ancient readers already felt the count was tight. Whether one calls Matthew's procedure a "manipulation" or a "stylized structure" is largely a matter of register; what is clear is that the scheme is numerological and that the historical sequence has been compressed to serve it.

The fair verdict is that the apparent shortfall dissolves once the pivot-counting and the deliberate gematria design are recognized — the forty-two is reached by counting boundary figures in both adjacent panels, which Matthew's structure both permits and, arguably, intends. But the resolution is purchased at the cost of historical completeness: three real kings are missing, and "forty-two generations" means forty-two scheme-positions, not forty-two distinct men. Verdict: overstated as a flat contradiction; the count is harmonizable through Matthew's own triadic gematria, but only by admitting the genealogy is theological architecture, not arithmetic.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Matthew's 3×14 scheme is gematria-driven (David = 14) and uses David and Jechoniah as pivot figures counted in two adjacent epochs each; counting the boundary figures twice yields 42 scheme-positions across the three panels, so the stated total coheres with the list once the genealogy is read as a stylized theological structure rather than a list of distinct begettings.

entries.question: Was Joseph the father of Jesus?
entries.books_in_tension: Matthew, Luke, Acts, Romans, 2 Timothy, Hebrews, Revelation
entries.summary: Acts 2:30, Acts 13:23, Romans 1:3, 2 Timothy 2:8, Hebrews 2:16, and Revelation 22:16 all describe Jesus as physically descended from David 'according to the flesh.' Davidic descent in this canon runs exclusively through Joseph (Matt 1:6-16; Luke 3:23-31 both trace it through him). But Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:31-35 say Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit and Joseph was not the biological father. If Joseph wasn't the father, the Davidic descent claim has no biological mechanism.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that virgin-birth Christology built into itself the moment it landed in a canon that also insists on Davidic descent *kata sarka*.

Paul says it plainly in Romans 1:3 — Jesus *tou genomenou ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka* (born of the seed of David according to the flesh). The phrase *kata sarka* (according to the flesh) is not metaphorical here — Paul contrasts it with *kata pneuma hagiōsynēs* (according to the spirit of holiness) in the next verse. The fleshly mechanism is genealogical inheritance through male line. That was how 'seed of David' worked in Second Temple messianism (cf. 4QFlor; *Psalms of Solomon* 17).

Matthew and Luke both give genealogies that run through Joseph (not Mary) precisely because that's how Davidic descent is established. Then Matthew 1:18 says *eurethē en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou* — 'she was found with child of the Holy Spirit' — and Luke 1:35 has the angel say *pneuma hagion epeleusetai epi se* — 'the Holy Spirit will come upon you.' Joseph is removed from the biological chain. So either the Davidic-descent claim collapses, or Joseph is the biological father after all.

The standard apologist harmonization is adoption: Jesus was Joseph's *legal* son under Jewish law, and legal sonship transmits inheritance rights including the Davidic claim. Brown discusses this carefully in *Birth of the Messiah* (pp. 138-139). It works for inheritance — Joseph naming the child (Matt 1:25, Luke 2:21) is the formal act of paternal acknowledgment. But it doesn't work for *kata sarka*. Paul, the author of Acts, the author of Hebrews, and John of Patmos are not making a legal-inheritance claim — they're making a fleshly-descent claim. 'Seed of David according to the flesh' is biology, not adoption law.

An alternative harmonization (the one developed in late antiquity and codified in Justin and Irenaeus) is that Mary herself was secretly of Davidic descent, transmitting the Davidic gene through her. But neither Matthew nor Luke says this — they give Joseph's genealogy, not Mary's. The Mary-Davidic-descent claim is a post-canonical patch.

Verdict: the canon claims both that Jesus is Joseph's biological flesh-descendant of David and that Joseph is not Jesus's biological father. Pick one.

commentary_out.commentary:
The tension is structural: the New Testament canon asserts both that Jesus is David's descendant *kata sarka* — by physical descent — and that Joseph, the only figure through whom either Gospel traces that Davidic descent, was not his biological father.

The Davidic claim is widespread and emphatic. Paul opens Romans with a formula most scholars judge to be pre-Pauline and creedal: Jesus *tou genomenou ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka* — "who came from the seed of David according to the flesh" (1:3). The phrase is not decorative. It stands in deliberate antithesis to *kata pneuma hagiōsynēs* in 1:4 ("according to the spirit of holiness"), the two-stage flesh/spirit contrast structuring the whole confession; *kata sarka* locates the Davidic descent in the ordinary human, fleshly sphere. Jewett and Fitzmyer both read it as genealogical descent through the male line, which is how "seed of David" functioned in Second Temple messianism: 4QFlorilegium reads the "shoot of David" of the Nathan oracle (2 Sam 7) as a coming royal deliverer, and *Psalms of Solomon* 17 prays for a Davidic king to be raised up by physical succession. Acts 2:30 ("of the fruit of his loins"), Acts 13:23, 2 Timothy 2:8, and Revelation 22:16 ("the root and offspring of David") echo the same biological-dynastic logic. Both Gospel genealogies establish that descent through Joseph — Matthew through the royal Solomonic line (1:6-16), Luke through Nathan (3:23-31) — not through Mary.

The virginal-conception narratives then sever Joseph from the biological chain. Matthew 1:18 says Mary was found *en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou* — "with child of the Holy Spirit" — before she and Joseph came together, and 1:25 specifies that Joseph "knew her not" until after the birth. Luke 1:34-35 has Mary protest that she "knows no man," and the angel answer that the Holy Spirit will come upon her. If Joseph supplies no "seed," the *kata sarka* descent through Joseph has no physical mechanism.

The strongest harmonization is legal adoption. Under Jewish custom, paternal acknowledgment — Joseph naming the child (Matt 1:25; cf. Luke 2:21) — confers full sonship, including inheritance and lineage rights. Brown lays this out fairly (pp. 138-139): Jesus is Joseph's legal son and therefore legally a son of David, and royal/messianic claims in antiquity were transmitted by legal standing, not genetics. This genuinely resolves the *dynastic* question. What it cannot resolve is the *fleshly* one. The creedal formula Paul cites does not say "of the house of David" or "reckoned to David" but "of the seed of David *according to the flesh*," set against "according to the spirit" — and adoption is precisely not a fleshly relation. The authors of Acts, Romans, Hebrews, and Revelation are not making an adoption-law claim; they are making a descent claim, and adoption supplies legal paternity, not flesh.

The second harmonization, that Mary herself was of Davidic descent, would supply the missing biology. But neither Matthew nor Luke says so; both give Joseph's line and present Mary's Davidic status nowhere. The claim is a post-canonical development: it surfaces in Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho* 43, 100) and Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 3.21.5), who assert Mary's Davidic descent precisely to close this gap, and the second-century *Protevangelium of James* makes her a daughter of the house of David. Lincoln's monograph documents how the early church reached for Mary's lineage exactly because the canonical texts left the *kata sarka* claim mechanically unsupported once Joseph was removed.

Verdict: genuine, canon-internal contradiction. Legal adoption rescues Jesus's *dynastic* Davidic title but not the repeated, creedally fixed claim of descent "according to the flesh"; the patch that would rescue the flesh-claim — Mary's own Davidic descent — is read into, not out of, the Gospels.

entries.question: Did Jesus baptize anyone?
entries.summary: John 3:22 says Jesus and his disciples went into the land of Judea and 'there he tarried with them, and baptized' — Jesus is the explicit subject of the baptizing verb. John 4:2 then says 'though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples.' The same gospel, two chapters apart, asserts opposite claims about whether Jesus performed baptisms.
entries.commentary:
This is the rare case where the contradiction is internal to a single book — John 3:22 vs. John 4:2 — and the author or a redactor seems to have noticed.

John 3:22: *ēlthen ho Iēsous kai hoi mathētai autou eis tēn Ioudaian gēn, kai ekei dietriben met' autōn kai ebaptizen* — 'Jesus came, and his disciples, into the Judean land, and there he was staying with them and was baptizing.' Singular verb *ebaptizen* (he was baptizing), with Jesus as the antecedent. The natural reading is that Jesus himself was baptizing.

John 4:2: *kaitoige Iēsous autos ouk ebaptizen all' hoi mathētai autou* — 'although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples (did).' This is a direct contradiction of the most natural reading of 3:22.

The traditional harmonization — Augustine, Calvin, and reaffirmed by modern apologists like Carson and Köstenberger — is that 3:22 uses *ebaptizen* loosely to mean 'Jesus's group was baptizing,' with Jesus as the representative subject for the activity his disciples actually performed. The harmonization is grammatically conceivable (you can describe a leader as 'doing' what his subordinates do under his authority) but doesn't fit the way the rest of John 3:22-26 reads. The crowds in 3:26 explicitly identify the baptizer as the one who was with John 'beyond the Jordan' — that's clearly Jesus personally, not just his group.

The near-universal critical reading (Brown AB John, Bultmann's *The Gospel of John*, Schnackenburg's HTKNT) is that John 4:2 is a redactional gloss — an editorial parenthesis inserted at some point during the gospel's composition to correct what the redactor saw as a theological problem in 3:22. Why the correction? Because by the time the Fourth Gospel was reaching its final form, the Christian community had developed sacramental theology in which baptism is performed *into* Christ, not *by* Christ — and the idea of Jesus personally baptizing disrupted the developing sacramental framework.

The textual evidence supports the gloss-hypothesis: 4:2 is syntactically awkward, breaks the flow between 4:1 and 4:3, and uses *kaitoige* (although) — a particle that signals correction or qualification. Brown calls 4:2 a 'parenthetical remark inserted to correct a possible misimpression' (AB 29, p. 164).

Verdict: 3:22 says Jesus baptized. 4:2 says he didn't. The 'representative subject' harmonization tortures 3:22's grammar. The critical reading — that 4:2 is a later editorial gloss correcting an earlier tradition — is the parsimonious explanation. Either way, the canonical text says both things.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is the rare case where the tension is wholly internal to a single book — John 3:22 versus John 4:2 — and where the author, or more probably a later hand in the gospel's layered composition, seems already to have registered the problem and tried to fix it.

John 3:22 reads: *ēlthen ho Iēsous kai hoi mathētai autou eis tēn Ioudaian gēn, kai ekei dietriben met' autōn kai ebaptizen* — 'Jesus came, and his disciples, into the Judean land, and there he was staying with them and was baptizing.' The verb *ebaptizen* is third-person singular imperfect, and its grammatical subject is Jesus. The most natural reading is that Jesus personally was conducting baptisms in Judea, in parallel and apparent competition with John the Baptist, who is described baptizing at Aenon near Salim a few verses later (3:23).

The surrounding material reinforces that this is Jesus himself. In 3:26 John's disciples come to him complaining: 'the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified — here he is baptizing, and all are going to him.' The complaint only stings if Jesus, the figure John had identified at the Jordan, is personally baptizing and drawing crowds. The whole pericope (3:22-30) is structured as a Baptist-versus-Jesus comparison, climaxing in John's confession that 'he must increase, but I must decrease.'

John 4:1-3 then narrates that the Pharisees heard 'that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John,' and the text interrupts itself with a parenthesis: *kaitoige Iēsous autos ouk ebaptizen all' hoi mathētai autou* — 'although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples (were).' This flatly negates the plain sense of 3:22.

The traditional harmonization — found in Augustine, Calvin, and reaffirmed by Carson and Köstenberger — reads 3:22 loosely: Jesus 'baptized' in the sense that his disciples baptized under his authority, the way one might say a general 'took the city' that his troops actually stormed. The representative-subject idiom is genuine Greek usage, and the harmonization is grammatically conceivable. But it strains against the immediate context. John 3:26's witnesses identify the baptizer specifically as the man who had stood with John at the Jordan — that is Jesus as an individual, not an undifferentiated 'group.' And if 3:22 were already understood as 'his disciples baptized,' the corrective gloss in 4:2 would be redundant; its very presence signals that someone read 3:22 as the text most naturally reads it and felt compelled to qualify it.

The near-universal critical reading (Brown, Bultmann, Schnackenburg) is that 4:2 is a redactional gloss — an editorial parenthesis inserted during the gospel's composition to correct a perceived problem in the earlier tradition. Three features support this. First, syntax: 4:2 disrupts the flow between 4:1 and 4:3, so that 4:3 ('he left Judea') resumes the subject of 4:1 awkwardly across the insertion. Second, the particle *kaitoige* ('and yet,' 'although'), rare in John, signals concession and correction. Third, the shift to the third person plural for the disciples sits uneasily with 4:1's singular focus on Jesus. Brown labels 4:2 a 'parenthetical remark... added to correct a misimpression that might be gained from iii 22' (Anchor Bible 29, p. 164).

Why correct it? Brown and Bultmann locate the motive in developing sacramental theology: as baptism came to be understood as incorporation *into* Christ, the picture of Jesus personally administering it became theologically awkward — one is baptized into Christ, not by him alongside John. The gloss protects that developing framework while leaving the older tradition embedded in 3:22.

Verdict: genuine internal tension, most economically explained as a later editorial gloss (4:2) correcting an earlier statement (3:22). The representative-subject harmonization is possible but forces the grammar; either way the canonical text asserts both that Jesus baptized and that he did not.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: If 3:22's *ebaptizen* is read as a representative-subject idiom ('Jesus baptized' = his disciples baptized under his authority), the two verses cohere; but the corrective gloss in 4:2 itself implies an editor read 3:22 in its plain personal sense.

entries.question: How did God address Jesus at his baptism?
entries.summary: Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 have the heavenly voice address Jesus directly in the second person: 'You are my beloved Son' (*sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos*). Matthew 3:17 has the voice address the crowd in the third person: 'This is my beloved Son' (*houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos*). The same theophany is reported with two different addressees.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook redactional contradiction — small, well-attested, and revealing of how the gospels relate to one another.

Mark 1:11 (the earliest gospel): *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — 'you are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.' Second person direct address. The voice speaks to Jesus.

Luke 3:22 follows Mark almost verbatim: *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — same construction. Second person.

Matthew 3:17 changes it: *houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos, en hō eudokēsa* — 'this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' Third person. The voice speaks *about* Jesus to whoever is listening.

The apologist harmonization runs two ways. Path one: the voice said both things — 'you are my Son' to Jesus and then 'this is my Son' to the bystanders. Two separate utterances. Possible in the abstract but unsupported by any single text, and runs into the problem that all three synoptics narrate this as a single voice-event, not two.

Path two (more sophisticated): the change from *sy ei* to *houtos estin* is a translation/paraphrase issue, with one or both forms preserving the underlying Aramaic ambiguity. This is a stretch — the Greek is unambiguous in each case, and Matthew is demonstrably editing Mark, not translating an independent source.

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison, Luz, Marcus, Fitzmyer) is that Matthew has redactionally altered Mark's second-person voice to a third-person public declaration. Why? Because Matthew's baptism scene has a different theological purpose than Mark's. In Mark, the voice is a private revelation to Jesus (only Jesus 'sees the heavens torn open,' 1:10) — it's about Jesus's commissioning. In Matthew, the voice is a public proclamation to anyone present (the heavens are 'opened to him' but the announcement is broadcast) — it's about Jesus's public identification as Son.

Luke, working with both Mark and Q-or-Matthew (depending on which Synoptic theory you prefer), preserves Mark's second-person form. This pattern — Luke siding with Mark against Matthew's edits — is a recurring feature that supports Markan priority and Lukan independence from Matthew.

The contradiction is not about whether the heavens spoke. It's about whether the voice addressed Jesus or the witnesses. Mark and Luke say one thing; Matthew says another. They cannot both be verbatim accurate to a single utterance.

Verdict: Matthew has redactionally changed Mark's second-person address into a third-person declaration. The harmonization that says 'both things were said' has no textual support. The parsimonious reading is that Matthew edited his source for theological reasons.

Note on the SAB answer labels: the 'Yes'/'No' labels in the source data are malformed for this question — they don't track the actual semantic distinction (direct address vs. announcement-to-bystanders). The contradiction substance is real even though the labels are confused.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is a textbook redactional contradiction — small, well-attested, and diagnostic of how the Synoptics relate to one another.

Mark 1:11, in the earliest gospel, reads *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — 'you are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.' The pronoun *sy* and the second-person verb make this direct address: the voice speaks to Jesus. The framing reinforces privacy — in 1:10 it is Jesus who 'saw the heavens being torn apart' (*schizomenous*) and the Spirit descending 'into him' (*eis auton*); the vision and the voice are oriented toward Jesus as recipient. Mark's scene functions as a commissioning theophany experienced by Jesus.

Luke 3:22 follows Mark almost verbatim: *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — second person, identical construction. (A famous Western variant, attested in Codex Bezae and several Fathers, has the voice quote Psalm 2:7 in full: 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.' That variant, whatever its origin, is still second-person direct address and does not affect the Matthew-versus-Mark/Luke contrast.)

Matthew 3:17 alters the form: *houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos, en hō eudokēsa* — 'this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' The demonstrative *houtos* and the third-person verb make this an announcement *about* Jesus, addressed to whoever is present. Matthew also generalizes the vision: the heavens 'were opened' (3:16) without Mark's violent tearing, and the declaration is broadcast publicly.

Two harmonizations are offered. The first: the voice said both — 'you are my Son' to Jesus and 'this is my Son' to the bystanders, two utterances compressed by different evangelists. This is conceivable in the abstract but textually unsupported; all three Synoptics narrate a single voice-event, and no account hints at a double pronouncement. The second, more sophisticated: that *sy ei* and *houtos estin* both render an underlying Aramaic original whose deixis was looser. This founders on the fact that each Greek form is unambiguous and that Matthew is demonstrably editing Mark's Greek text rather than independently translating a Semitic source — the verbal agreement is too close for independent translation.

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison, Luz, Marcus, Fitzmyer) is that Matthew redactionally converted Mark's second-person private revelation into a third-person public proclamation, consistent with Matthew's broader presentation of the baptism as Jesus's public identification (note the dialogue with John in 3:14-15, unique to Matthew, which frames the event for an audience). Mark's scene is about Jesus's own commissioning; Matthew's is about Jesus's public attestation as Son.

Luke's retention of Mark's second-person form is itself significant. On the Two-Source theory, Luke's siding with Mark against Matthew's redaction is one of many minor pieces of evidence for Markan priority and for Luke's independence from Matthew — if Luke had known and followed Matthew, the third-person form would be hard to explain.

The contradiction is not whether a heavenly voice spoke, nor what it said about Jesus's sonship; it is the addressee. Mark and Luke have God speak to Jesus; Matthew has God speak about Jesus to the witnesses. A single utterance cannot be both second-person and third-person.

Verdict: genuine compositional contradiction, best explained as Matthean redaction of Mark for theological emphasis; the 'both were spoken' harmonization has no textual warrant.
