entries.question: Is anyone good?
entries.summary: Isaiah 64:6 says all human righteousness is *kĕbeged ʿiddîm* — 'as filthy rags' — and the Pauline literature builds an entire doctrine of universal depravity on this and similar verses. Luke 23:50 then describes Joseph of Arimathea as *anēr agathos kai dikaios* — 'a good and just man.' The same canon that insists no one is good has narrators describing specific individuals as good.
entries.commentary:
This is a question about whether the Bible's universal-depravity passages and its particular-virtue descriptions can be held in the same hand. The apologist response actually works pretty well for most of the canon — Luke 23:50 is the awkward outlier.

Isaiah 64:6 (MT 64:5) in context is a communal lament about exilic Israel's collective failure — *wattĕmaʿăṭēnû bĕyad-ʿăwōnēnû* — 'and you have melted us in the hand of our iniquity.' The 'filthy rags' line is a corporate confession in a specific historical moment, not a metaphysical statement about every individual being incapable of any virtue. Reading it as universal anthropological pessimism (the Augustinian/Calvinist move) requires lifting it out of its lament-genre context.

Paul does something similar in Romans 3:10-12, quoting Psalm 14:1-3 ('there is none who does good, no not one'). The Psalm in its original Hebrew context is about *bĕnê ʾādām* who have gone astray, not a metaphysical claim that no human being can ever be virtuous. Romans 3 weaponizes it for theological purposes.

Meanwhile the Hebrew Bible repeatedly describes specific people as *ṣaddîq* (righteous): Noah was *ʾîš ṣaddîq tāmîm hāyāh bĕdōrōtāyw* — 'a righteous man, blameless in his generations' (Gen 6:9). Job is described by God himself as *ʾîš tām wĕyāšār* — 'blameless and upright' (Job 1:8). Luke 1:6 calls Zechariah and Elizabeth *dikaioi amphoteroi enantion tou theou* — 'both righteous before God.' And Luke 23:50 calls Joseph of Arimathea *anēr agathos kai dikaios*.

More directly relevant: Jesus in Mark 10:18 (and Luke 18:19) responds to being called 'good teacher' with *ti me legeis agathon? oudeis agathos ei mē heis ho theos* — 'why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.' That's a clean denial that anyone but God is *agathos*. Luke himself then turns around in 23:50 and uses *agathos* of Joseph of Arimathea. Luke contradicts Luke's own Jesus.

The apologist harmonization — Carson, Bock BECNT Luke, the IVP *Hard Sayings* commentary — distinguishes between (1) relative goodness (humans compared to other humans) and (2) absolute goodness (only God). On that reading Joseph of Arimathea is relatively good while still being unable to claim absolute goodness in God's sight. Same word, two senses.

The distinction is real in theology but the Greek text doesn't mark it. *Agathos* is *agathos*. When Luke applies it to Joseph and Jesus denies it of everyone but God, the same lexical item is doing both jobs. The contradiction is in the canon's flat-footed use of the same word.

Verdict: the lament-genre context softens Isaiah 64:6 significantly. The harder problem is Jesus's *oudeis agathos* in Mark 10:18/Luke 18:19 vs. Luke 23:50's *anēr agathos*. The relative-vs-absolute defense works as theology but doesn't track the Greek vocabulary the texts actually use.

commentary_out.commentary:
The question is whether the canon's universal-depravity statements and its particular-virtue descriptions can be held together. The honest answer is that the Old Testament side largely resolves on genre, while the harder residue is an internal Lukan one involving a single Greek word.

Isaiah 64:6 (MT 64:5) belongs to a communal lament. The surrounding verses plead with a God who has 'hidden his face' (64:7) over a people in exile: *wattĕmaʿăṭēnû bĕyad-ʿăwōnēnû* — 'and you have melted us into the hand of our iniquity.' The image *kĕbeged ʿiddîm* — 'like a menstruous/soiled garment' — describes the collective state of a guilty nation in a specific historical moment, not a metaphysical claim that no individual can possess any virtue. Blenkinsopp and Westermann both read it as corporate confession within the Trito-Isaianic lament, and to make it a universal anthropology (the Augustinian and later Calvinist use) is to lift it from its genre. The same caution applies to Paul's catena in Romans 3:10-12, which strings together Psalm 14:1-3 and other texts; Fitzmyer notes that Paul reapplies originally particular or hyperbolic statements to a universal forensic argument about Jew and Gentile alike standing 'under sin.' The Hebrew Psalm targets a class of fools and evildoers, not literally every human.

Meanwhile the Hebrew Bible cheerfully calls specific people righteous: Noah is *ʾîš ṣaddîq tāmîm* (Gen 6:9), Job is declared *tām wĕyāšār* by God himself (Job 1:8), and Luke 1:6 calls Zechariah and Elizabeth *dikaioi ... enantion tou theou*. Luke 23:50 describes Joseph of Arimathea as *anēr agathos kai dikaios* — 'a good and righteous man.'

The sharper problem is internal to Luke. In Luke 18:19 (paralleling Mark 10:18) Jesus responds to the address 'good teacher' with *ti me legeis agathon? oudeis agathos ei mē heis ho theos* — 'why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.' That is a flat denial of *agathos* to anyone but God. Yet the same author, five chapters later, applies *agathos* to Joseph of Arimathea. Marcus and Fitzmyer both note the theological awkwardness of the Markan saying — so much so that Matthew 19:17 rewrites it to blunt the implication ('Why do you ask me about what is good?'), a redactional tell that early scribes and evangelists already felt the tension.

The standard apologetic move — Bock, the IVP *Hard Sayings* tradition, and Carson — distinguishes absolute goodness (God alone) from relative or derivative goodness (humans being called good in a qualified sense). Theologically this is coherent: Joseph can be 'good' as a creature without claiming the unqualified moral perfection that belongs to God. The difficulty is that the Greek text does not mark the distinction. *Agathos* in Luke 18:19 and *agathos* in Luke 23:50 are the same lexeme with no qualifier; the relative/absolute split is supplied by the interpreter, not by the syntax. Where Luke wanted to qualify, as in 18:19, he could and did ('except God alone'); in 23:50 he does not.

Verdict: overstated on the Old Testament side, where the lament and Psalm genres dissolve the apparent universal claim; partially harmonized overall, since the relative-vs-absolute distinction is theologically sound but is not encoded in the shared Greek vocabulary of Luke 18:19 and 23:50, leaving a residual lexical tension Matthew himself smoothed.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Isaiah 64:6 and the Romans 3 catena are communal-lament and hyperbolic-Psalm material, not universal anthropology, so the OT 'no one is good' reading is a genre misreading; the residual Luke 18:19 vs 23:50 tension is reconcilable in theology by an absolute-vs-relative sense of agathos, but that distinction is interpretive rather than marked in the shared Greek, so the harmonization is only partial — corroborated by Matthew 19:17's redactional softening of the same saying.

entries.question: Should Christians be concerned with material things?
entries.summary: Matthew 6:31, 34 has Jesus instruct disciples to take no thought (*mē merimnēsēte*) for food, drink, clothing, or the morrow. 1 Timothy 5:8 then says if anyone *tōn idiōn kai malista oikeiōn ou pronoei, tēn pistin ērnētai* — 'does not provide for his own, especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' One text forbids material anxiety; the other makes material provision a test of authentic faith.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction turns on the semantic range of the Greek words involved, and the apologist response does meaningful lexical work — but the underlying tension between Synoptic ethics and Pastoral ethics is real and well-documented in critical scholarship.

Matthew 6:25-34 uses *merimnaō* — to be anxious, to worry. The instruction is *mē merimnāte tē psychē hymōn* — 'do not be anxious for your life' — about what you'll eat, drink, wear. The reasoning is providential: the birds don't sow and the lilies don't spin, and the Father provides for them. Disciples are to seek first the kingdom and let tomorrow worry about itself.

1 Timothy 5:8 uses a different word: *pronoeō* — to plan ahead, to provide for, to take forethought for. Specifically *idiōn kai malista oikeiōn* — 'one's own, especially household.' The instruction is positive provision-making for dependent family members.

The apologist harmonization — Mounce on the Pastorals, Marshall ICC on the Pastorals, France NICNT Matthew — distinguishes (1) *merimna*-style anxiety, which is paralyzing fear about basic survival, from (2) *pronoia*-style forethought, which is responsible planning for dependents. Same lexical field is not the same instruction. Jesus condemns anxious distrust of God's provision; the Pastor commands prudent household management. No contradiction at the Greek lexical level.

This is a credible distinction. The Greek words really are different, and the conceptual fields really are distinguishable. *Merimna* is the worry that consumes; *pronoia* is the planning that enables. Stoic ethics worked with similar distinctions.

But the apologist defense glosses over how *demanding* Matthew 6:31-34 actually is. *Mē merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion* — 'do not be anxious about tomorrow' — combined with the parable's logic (the birds don't sow and reap, you should be even more cared for) is hard to square with running a household budget, planning for children's needs, saving against illness. The instruction isn't 'don't worry obsessively while still planning prudently'; it's 'consider the lilies — they neither toil nor spin.' Taken at face value, this is a radical eschatological ethic that presupposes the imminent kingdom is about to break in and ordinary economic forethought is obsolete.

The critical reading (Allison *The End of the Ages Has Come*; Theissen *The First Followers of Jesus*; Crossan *The Historical Jesus*) is that Matthew 6 preserves a genuine pre-70 Jesus-tradition wandering-charismatic ethic. Jesus and his early followers were itinerant prophets who did not work, did not save, and did not provide for households because they expected the end imminently. The Pastoral Epistles (whether or not authentically Pauline; the critical consensus is post-Pauline pseudepigrapha) reflect a second- or third-generation settled-church ethic where households need to be maintained over decades and the eschatological clock has slowed.

The lexical distinction between *merimna* and *pronoia* papers over what is genuinely a development from charismatic itinerancy to institutional household-Christianity. Both traditions are preserved in the canon. They don't fully cohere.

Verdict: the lexical distinction softens the surface contradiction in a defensible way. The underlying tension — Jesus's wandering-prophet ethic vs. the Pastorals' settled-household ethic — is real and is one of the standard fault lines critical scholarship has identified across the New Testament.

commentary_out.commentary:
The harmonization here does genuine lexical work, but it cannot fully cover a tension that critical scholarship has long identified as a fault line between Synoptic and Pastoral ethics.

Matthew 6:25-34 turns on *merimnaō* — to be anxious, to be inwardly torn, to worry. The imperative is *mē merimnāte tē psychē hymōn* — 'do not be anxious about your life' — as to what you will eat, drink, or wear. The argument is providential and rhetorical: the birds *ou speirousin oude therizousin* ('neither sow nor reap') yet the Father feeds them; the lilies *ou kopiōsin oude nēthousin* ('neither toil nor spin') yet are clothed more gloriously than Solomon. The conclusion is *mē merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion* — 'do not be anxious about tomorrow.' Disciples are to *zēteite de prōton tēn basileian* — 'seek first the kingdom.'

1 Timothy 5:8 uses a different verb: *pronoeō* — to think ahead, to provide, to take forethought — and a different object, *tōn idiōn kai malista oikeiōn* ('one's own, and especially household members'). The failure to provide is so grave it amounts to having *tēn pistin ērnētai* ('denied the faith') and being worse than *apistos* ('an unbeliever'). The context (5:3-16) is the concrete administration of the widow-roll, an institutional welfare problem in a settled congregation.

The harmonizing case (Marshall, Mounce, France) distinguishes anxiety from forethought. *Merimna* names the paralyzing, faith-corroding fear about basic survival; *pronoia* names the responsible planning a head of household owes dependents. The Greek terms genuinely differ, and the conceptual distinction is real — Stoic moral psychology drew comparable lines between destructive *pathos* and rational *prohairesis*. On this reading Jesus condemns distrustful worry, the Pastor commands prudent provision, and no contradiction arises at the lexical level. This is a credible and partially successful move.

What it understates is how demanding Matthew 6:31-34 actually is. The instruction is not 'plan prudently while refusing to fret'; it is 'consider the lilies — they neither toil nor spin.' The illustrative logic explicitly contrasts disciples with creatures that do *not* labor, sow, or store, and asks them to trust accordingly. Taken at face value this is a radical ethic that presupposes the imminent in-breaking of the kingdom and the obsolescence of ordinary economic forethought (Luz; Allison). It coheres with the sending instructions to take no bag, no bread, no money (Mark 6:8; Luke 9:3; 10:4) — an itinerant pattern, not a household budget.

The critical reading (Theissen; Allison; Crossan) is that Matthew 6 preserves an early, pre-70 wandering-charismatic ethic. Jesus and his first followers were itinerant prophets who did not work, save, or maintain households, because they expected the end soon. The Pastoral Epistles, which the dominant critical consensus regards as post-Pauline pseudepigrapha from the late first or early second century (Marshall is a notable dissenter arguing for an 'allonymous' Pauline circle), reflect a settled, institutional Christianity in which households persist over decades, congregations administer welfare rolls, and the eschatological clock has slowed. The shift Theissen labels the move from 'wandering charismatics' to 'local communities' is precisely the shift between these two texts. The *merimna*/*pronoia* distinction is real, but it papers over a development in social setting and eschatological expectation that the canon preserves without reconciling.

Verdict: the lexical distinction defensibly softens the surface clash. The underlying tension — Jesus's itinerant-prophet ethic versus the Pastorals' settled-household ethic — is genuine and is one of the standard developmental seams critical scholarship maps across the New Testament. Partially harmonizable.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The two texts use different Greek verbs targeting different attitudes: Matthew 6 forbids merimnaō ('to be anxious, consumed by worry') about survival, distrusting God's provision, while 1 Timothy 5:8 commands pronoeō ('to take prudent forethought, provide') for dependents. The lexical fields are distinguishable, so the surface contradiction softens. The harmonization is partial only because Matthew 6's radical 'consider the lilies' rhetoric presupposes imminent-kingdom expectation that does not fully accommodate ordinary household economics.

entries.question: Was Jairus's daughter alive when Jesus was approached?
entries.summary: Mark 5:22-23 and Luke 8:41-42 have the synagogue ruler (Mark and Luke name him Jairus) come to Jesus while his daughter is still alive — "at the point of death" / "a dying." Matthew 9:18 has the same ruler approach Jesus and announce that his daughter is "even now dead" (Greek *arti eteleutēsen*). The same scene, the same petitioner, two incompatible reports about whether the girl was alive or already dead at the moment of the request.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest demonstrations of Matthean redactional compression in the Synoptic problem. Mark's version (the source) runs the story in two stages: Jairus comes while the daughter is dying, then messengers arrive partway through to report she has died (Mark 5:35). Luke follows Mark almost exactly. Matthew collapses the two stages into one — by the time the ruler speaks, the daughter is already dead. The apologist harmonization (Archer, Geisler-Howe) argues that Matthew is just "summarizing" or "telescoping" the events, and that the ruler's statement reflects his certainty that by now she must be dead. That reading works only if you ignore the Greek. Matthew uses *arti eteleutēsen* — "she just died" — an aorist of immediate completion, not a hypothetical. The ruler is reporting a death, not predicting one. Critical scholarship (Davies-Allison, Luz, Hagner) reads this as a deliberate Matthean abbreviation that serves a narrative purpose: it makes the miracle bigger (raising from death rather than healing the dying) and removes the messenger-interruption that complicated Mark's narrative. The harmonization that the ruler "assumed" she had died by the time he reached Jesus is post-hoc rationalization — the text says he reported a death, not a probable death. That is of course a judgment about Greek tense, but the tense is what it is.

answers.answer_explanation: While he spake these things unto them, behold, there came a certain ruler, and worshipped him, saying, My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live. Matthew 9:18

And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet, And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: I pray thee, come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live. Mark 5:22-23

And, behold, there came a man named Jairus, and he was a ruler of the synagogue: and he fell down at Jesus' feet, and besought him that he would come into his house: For he had one only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she lay a dying. Luke 8:41-42

commentary_out.commentary:
The story of the synagogue ruler and his daughter is one of the cleanest demonstrations of Matthean redactional compression available in the Synoptic tradition, and the tension between the three accounts is grammatical, not merely impressionistic. Mark, on the priority hypothesis the source text, structures the episode in two distinct stages. First, Jairus comes to Jesus while his daughter is still alive: "my little daughter lies at the point of death" (eschatōs echei, Mark 5:23). Then, while Jesus is delayed by the hemorrhaging woman, messengers arrive from the house with the news, "Your daughter is dead" (Mark 5:35). The death is narrated as an event that occurs partway through the pericope; the petition and the death are separated by the intercalated healing of the woman. Luke 8:41-42 follows Mark closely, keeping the two-stage structure intact ("she lay a-dying") and likewise placing the report of death later (Luke 8:49).

Matthew collapses the two stages into one. By the time the ruler — unnamed in Matthew, who omits Jairus — opens his mouth, the girl is already dead: "My daughter has just now died (arti eteleutēsen), but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live" (Matt 9:18). The contradiction sits squarely in the verb. Eteleutēsen is the aorist of teleutaō, "to die," and the adverb arti ("just now," "at this moment") pins the action to the immediate past. This is a report of a completed death, not a hypothetical or a fear. The ruler is not saying "she may be dead by now"; he is announcing that she has died.

The standard apologetic harmonization (Archer; Geisler and Howe) argues that Matthew is simply summarizing or "telescoping" the longer Markan narrative, and that the ruler's words reflect his reasonable assumption that, given the time elapsed, his daughter must by now have died. This reading is grammatically untenable. Arti eteleutēsen does not express probability or anticipation; Greek had ample resources for a future or a hypothetical (a future indicative, a conditional construction, or the adverb tacha, "perhaps"), and Matthew used none of them. The aorist of immediate completion reports an accomplished fact. A second apologetic move — that the ruler in Matthew is a different official altogether — founders on the close verbal and structural parallels and the embedded hemorrhaging-woman story common to all three, which mark this as one and the same tradition.

Critical scholarship (Davies and Allison; Luz; Hagner) reads the variation as a deliberate Matthean abbreviation serving a clear narrative and Christological purpose. By compressing the two stages, Matthew (1) eliminates the messenger interruption that complicates Mark's flow, and (2) magnifies the miracle: in Mark and Luke the petition is for a healing of one who is dying, and only later does it become a raising of one who has died; in Matthew it is, from the outset, a request to raise the dead. Matthew thereby front-loads the resurrection motif and heightens the demonstration of Jesus' authority over death. This is consistent with Matthew's broader tendency to abbreviate Markan miracle stories — his version of the whole pericope is roughly a third the length of Mark's — while sharpening their theological point.

The disagreement is real but small, and its origin is well understood: it is the predictable byproduct of a redactor compressing a two-stage source into a single scene. That such editing produces a factual discrepancy about whether the girl was alive or dead at the moment of the request is precisely the kind of evidence source critics cite for free editorial reworking of Mark by Matthew. The harmonization that the ruler merely "assumed" her death is post hoc rationalization that the Greek tense does not permit. Verdict: genuine contradiction arising from Matthean redactional compression of Mark.

issues.problem: The commentary characterizes 'arti eteleutēsen' as 'an aorist of immediate completion' that 'does not express probability or anticipation.' This overstates the grammatical case. The aorist with 'arti' does report a death, but the apologetic 'telescoping' argument is not primarily a grammatical claim about the verb tense — it is a claim that Matthew abbreviates by having the father state the outcome he has by now learned of (cf. the Markan messengers). Treating the harmonization purely as a mistaken tense-claim slightly strawmans the stronger form of the telescoping argument (which concedes the aorist but locates the compression at the level of narrative sequence, not verb mood). This is a borderline issue; the commentary does engage the telescoping argument substantively, so severity is medium-low.
issues.correction: Acknowledge that the strongest telescoping harmonization concedes 'arti eteleutēsen' is a real aorist of death and argues instead that Matthew has compressed the Markan two-stage report into a single utterance placed on the father's lips — i.e., the issue is narrative compression, not a misread tense. The commentary's verdict (genuine contradiction from redactional compression) can stand, but the apologetic case should be steel-manned as a compression argument rather than reduced to a tense error.

entries.question: Does the Bible approve of capital punishment?
entries.summary: The Pentateuchal legal codes prescribe death by stoning, burning, or general execution for an enormous range of offenses: murder (Gen 9:6; Num 35:30), striking or cursing a parent (Exod 21:15, 17), witchcraft (Exod 22:18), bestiality (Exod 22:19), idolatry (Exod 22:20), Sabbath-breaking (Exod 31:14-15; 35:2), adultery (Lev 20:10), incest (Lev 20:11-14), male homosexuality (Lev 20:13), blasphemy (Lev 24:16), kidnapping (Exod 21:16), loss of virginity before marriage (Deut 22:13-21), and rape victims who didn't cry out loudly enough (Deut 22:23-24). Genesis 4:15 has God explicitly *prevent* the execution of Cain — the first murderer — by placing a protective mark on him. The same canon both prescribes death for dozens of offenses and protects the prototypical murderer from execution.
entries.commentary: The question is framed as a binary yes/no, and at that level the answer is unambiguous: the Pentateuch overwhelmingly endorses capital punishment for a long catalog of offenses. Genesis 4:15 is the single anomalous data point, and it sits in a different narrative register — a pre-Sinai etiological story rather than a legal prescription. The apologist harmonization (Walton, Hamilton, Wenham, Sailhamer) reads Genesis 4:15 not as a divine disapproval of capital punishment but as a specific narrative provision protecting Cain from blood-revenge in the pre-Noahic era, before the institution of human juridical authority that Genesis 9:6 establishes ("by man shall his blood be shed"). On this reading, God's protection of Cain is consistent with the later Levitical legal framework because Cain lives in a pre-legal time when no institutional authority exists to execute him; the mark prevents private vengeance, not institutional justice. That's a defensible canonical reading and Walton and Hamilton are reasonable in advancing it. The deeper contradiction, though, is between the Pentateuchal death-penalty catalog and the New Testament Jesus, who in John 8:7 explicitly suspends a Mosaic capital sentence with "he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her" — a passage that is itself textually problematic (the pericope adulterae is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is a clear later addition to John, but the sentiment is preserved across multiple later witnesses). The actual binary the contradictions database is asking — "does the Bible approve capital punishment" — gets answered yes by the Pentateuch and complicated by the New Testament. Within the Pentateuchal frame alone, the prescriptions vastly outweigh Genesis 4:15, and most critical scholarship (Levenson, Knohl, Milgrom) reads the Holiness Code and the Covenant Code as straightforward endorsements of capital punishment. The contradiction is real if you read the canon as a unified ethical voice; less sharp if you read it as a layered legal tradition with development over time. That is of course a methodological choice.

commentary_out.commentary:
Posed as a binary, the question has an unambiguous answer for the Pentateuch: the legal codes endorse capital punishment for a long and varied catalog of offenses. The death penalty in the Torah is not a single law but the convergence of three distinct legal strata that source criticism distinguishes — the Covenant Code (Exod 20:22-23:33, including the execution provisions of 21:12-17, 22:18-20), the Holiness Code (Lev 17-26, supplying the dense list of capital offenses in Lev 20, with its refrain "their blood is upon them"), and the Deuteronomic law (Deut 22 and elsewhere). These corpora developed over time and in different circles — the Priestly/Holiness material is widely dated to the exilic or post-exilic period, the Covenant Code to an earlier monarchic setting — yet all three independently prescribe death, by stoning, burning, or unspecified execution, for offenses ranging from murder to Sabbath violation, idolatry, adultery, incest, male homosexual intercourse, blasphemy, cursing a parent, and a young bride found not to be a virgin. The cumulative weight is overwhelming endorsement.

Genesis 4:15, where the LORD sets a protective mark on Cain "lest any who found him should kill him," is the lone counter-text, and it sits in a fundamentally different register. It is not a legal prescription but a narrative etiology set in primeval, pre-Sinai time. The harmonization advanced by Walton, Hamilton, Wenham, and Sailhamer reads it accordingly: God protects Cain from private blood-vengeance in an era before any juridical institution exists to try and execute a murderer. This is wholly consistent with the later framework, which in Genesis 9:6 — itself part of the primeval narrative — establishes lethal human authority over bloodshed ("whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed"). On this reading the mark forestalls vendetta, not institutional justice; it does not express divine disapproval of capital punishment but the absence, in Cain's day, of the lawful authority to administer it. This is a sound canonical reading and the database's "No" answer overreads Genesis 4:15: the verse simply does not assert that God disapproves of capital punishment. As an internal Pentateuchal matter, then, the tension largely dissolves, because the death-penalty laws and the protection of Cain operate in different registers and different epochs of the narrative world.

The sharper tension is canonical and cross-testamental, and the existing commentary rightly points to it. In John 8:7 Jesus suspends the Mosaic stoning penalty for adultery ("Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her"), a scene whose moral force runs directly against Lev 20:10 and Deut 22. But this passage cannot bear much weight: the pericope adulterae (John 7:53-8:11) is textually secondary. It is absent from the earliest and best witnesses — P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus — appears at varied locations in the manuscripts that do carry it (some after Luke 21:38), and is marked with obeli in others; the critical consensus (Metzger, Ehrman) is that it was not part of the original Gospel of John, even if the underlying tradition may be old. As evidence for a canonical contradiction it is therefore compromised, though the sympathy it expresses recurs more broadly in early Christian ethics.

Whether the question yields a "contradiction" thus depends on a methodological choice. Read as a single, harmonized ethical voice, the Bible both prescribes death for dozens of acts and, in the Cain episode and the later Jesus tradition, restrains lethal punishment — a tension. Read as a layered, historically developing legal tradition — the approach of Milgrom, Knohl, Greenberg, and the comparative ANE work collected by Westbrook — the Pentateuchal codes are straightforward, culturally typical endorsements of capital punishment, broadly paralleled in the Laws of Hammurabi and other Near Eastern collections, while Genesis 4:15 is a narrative provision and the Johannine scene a late accretion. Within the Pentateuch itself, the prescriptions vastly outweigh the single counter-text, and that counter-text does not say what the contradiction requires.

Verdict: overstated within the Pentateuch — Genesis 4:15 is a pre-juridical narrative provision, not a divine repudiation of capital punishment; a real ethical tension exists only at the canonical level, and the strongest NT counter-text (John 8) is text-critically secondary.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Genesis 4:15 belongs to the pre-Sinai primeval narrative and protects Cain from private blood-vengeance in an era before juridical institutions existed (institutions Genesis 9:6 later establishes); it is a narrative provision, not a legal prohibition, and does not assert divine disapproval of capital punishment. The genuine ethical tension surfaces only when the canon is read as a unified voice and the Pentateuchal death-penalty laws are set against the Jesus tradition — but the sharpest NT counter-text, John 8:7, is text-critically secondary and absent from the earliest manuscripts.

entries.question: Did Jesus forewarn the apostles of his death and resurrection?
entries.summary: The Synoptic Gospels record Jesus making at least three explicit, detailed passion predictions to the disciples (Matt 16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19; Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34; Luke 9:22; 9:44; 18:31-33) — each one specifying betrayal, condemnation, death, and resurrection on the third day. John 20:9 then says, after the resurrection, "For as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead." If Jesus had personally told them three times that he would rise on the third day, John 20:9 is incomprehensible.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleaner cases where the Synoptic and Johannine narrative traditions can't both be reporting the same disciple-knowledge state. The Synoptic passion predictions are increasingly specific — by Mark 10:33-34, Jesus is naming the betrayal, the Gentile transfer, the mocking, the scourging, the death, and the third-day resurrection. The disciples' shock and confusion in the resurrection narratives only makes sense if they hadn't been told. John 20:9 makes this explicit. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg, France) runs through the "hidden from them" route: the disciples were told but didn't understand because the meaning was supernaturally hidden from them until after the resurrection. There is genuine textual support for this — Luke 9:45 says "they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them, that they perceived it not." Luke 18:34 repeats: "they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." So the Synoptic tradition itself contains a built-in mechanism for explaining the disciples' incomprehension. The harmonization mitigates the contradiction but doesn't dissolve it. John 20:9 doesn't say the disciples had been told and didn't understand; it says "as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead" — pointing to scriptural unfamiliarity, not to a forgotten teaching from Jesus. If Jesus had explicitly told them "on the third day I will rise," the post-resurrection problem wouldn't be scriptural ignorance; it would be remembering Jesus' words. Critical scholarship (Brown, Meier, Ehrman, Marcus) widely treats the detailed passion predictions as Markan vaticinia ex eventu — prophecies written after the fact and put into Jesus' mouth to demonstrate his foreknowledge. The disciples' apparent ignorance in the post-resurrection narratives, including John 20:9, is a residue of the historical situation where these predictions did not exist in the form the gospels later supplied them. That is of course a critical-historical judgment, but the Lukan "hidden from them" explanation reads as exactly the kind of editorial overlay that an early redactor adds when his source material contains a contradiction he needs to paper over.

commentary_out.commentary:
The Synoptic passion predictions are among the most schematized material in the Gospels. Mark frames three (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34), each more detailed than the last, building to the climactic 10:33-34, which names the betrayal, the handover to the chief priests and scribes, the condemnation, the transfer to the Gentiles, the mocking, scourging, spitting, killing, and resurrection "the third day." Matthew and Luke reproduce and in places sharpen these (Matt 16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19; Luke 9:22; 9:44; 18:31-33). Against this backdrop, John 20:9 reads as a flat contradiction: after the resurrection, "as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead." If Jesus had told the Twelve three times, with mounting precision, that he would rise on the third day, the disciples' post-resurrection bafflement is hard to credit.

Two features of John 20:9 deserve close attention. First, the object of the disciples' ignorance is *tēn graphēn* — "the scripture" — not Jesus' own predictive words. The Johannine narrator says the disciples had not yet grasped the scriptural necessity of resurrection, most likely an allusion to texts such as Psalm 16:10 ("thou wilt not leave my soul in hell") and Hosea 6:2 ("the third day he will raise us up"), which the early church read messianically (cf. Acts 2:25-31; 1 Cor 15:4). Second, the verb is *ēdeisan* (pluperfect of *oida*), "they had known/understood," framing this as a cognitive state only resolved by the resurrection appearances.

The strongest harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg, France) does not rest on special pleading; it rests on the Synoptic text itself. Luke twice inserts an explicit veiling motif: after the second prediction, "they understood not this saying, and it was hid (*parakekalymmenon*) from them, that they perceived it not" (9:45); and after the third, "they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them, neither knew they the things which were spoken" (18:34). The Synoptic tradition therefore furnishes its own mechanism: the disciples were told but, by something approaching divine concealment, failed to comprehend until after the event. On this reading John 20:9 is simply the Johannine version of the same incomprehension theme, and the apparent conflict largely dissolves. This is a genuinely strong point and is why the status here is partial rather than total.

What the harmonization does not quite reach is the specific content of John 20:9. The Lukan veiling explains why the disciples did not *understand* a teaching they had received; John locates the failure one step further back, in not yet knowing *the scripture* that resurrection was necessary. These are not identical claims. A disciple could fail to grasp Jesus' words yet, the moment the tomb was found empty, recall that Jesus had repeatedly said he would rise on the third day — which is precisely what Luke 24:6-8 has the angels prompt ("Remember how he spake unto you... the third day rise again. And they remembered his words"). John 20:9, by grounding the gap in scriptural rather than dominical ignorance, sits awkwardly with the explicit, thrice-repeated dominical predictions.

Critical scholarship (Brown, Meier, Marcus, Ehrman) widely regards the detailed third-day predictions as Markan *vaticinia ex eventu* — prophecies-after-the-fact retrojected to display Jesus' foreknowledge. The very precision of Mark 10:33-34, matching the passion narrative point for point, is the tell. On this view the disciples' historical incomprehension is authentic bedrock, and the explicit predictions are a later overlay; Luke's veiling clauses then function as redactional stitching to reconcile the inherited tradition of disciple-ignorance with the newly supplied predictions. John 20:9 preserves the older, prediction-free memory of disciples genuinely surprised by the resurrection. The contradiction is thus real at the level of the narrative as it now stands, but it is substantially mitigated by the Synoptics' own veiling motif. Verdict: partially harmonizable; the residual tension is John's appeal to scriptural rather than remembered ignorance.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Synoptic tradition itself supplies a built-in 'hidden from them' mechanism (Luke 9:45; 18:34) explaining the disciples' incomprehension despite being told, which substantially mitigates — though does not fully dissolve — John 20:9, since John grounds the failure in scriptural ignorance rather than forgotten teaching.

entries.question: What was Jesus' sixth commandment?
entries.summary: In the rich young ruler pericope, Jesus enumerates a list of commandments from the Decalogue. Matthew's list has six items ending with 'love thy neighbor as thyself' as number six. Mark's list also has six items but ends with 'honour thy father and mother' as number six and adds a non-Decalogue 'defraud not.' Luke's list has only five items and drops the parental commandment entirely from the sixth position. Three evangelists, three different versions of which commandment Jesus put sixth.
entries.commentary: The standard harmonization is that Jesus rattled off the commandments in slightly different orders on different occasions, or that each evangelist is offering a partial summary, not a transcript. The apologist version of this move shows up in Archer and in Blomberg's NAC Matthew. The problem is that the Synoptics are pretty clearly working from a common source here — Markan priority is the consensus position, and Matthew and Luke are demonstrably editing Mark. So the divergence isn't three independent eyewitness reports trailing off in different directions. It's two later editors reshaping the source. Mark's order (adultery, kill, steal, false witness, defraud not, honour parents) actually inverts the LXX/MT order on murder and adultery and inserts 'defraud not,' which isn't in the Decalogue at all — Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark notes the 'defraud not' is likely a gloss reflecting either the tenth commandment on coveting or Sirach 4:1. Matthew (NAC) cleans Mark up: restores the canonical order, drops 'defraud not,' and adds the second great commandment 'love thy neighbor' as a climax — because Matthew wants the encounter to telescope into the Great Commandment debate later in his gospel. Luke shortens the list and reorders. Each evangelist is shaping the tradition to fit his theological program. That's not a transcript problem, that's redaction. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, you can argue Jesus said different things on different occasions. But the three accounts are clearly the *same* pericope — same young man, same wealth question, same answer about selling possessions — so 'different occasions' doesn't survive contact with the parallel structure. Take your pick: redaction or three separate near-identical interviews.

commentary_out.commentary:
All three Synoptics narrate the same encounter — a wealthy inquirer asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus directs him to the commandments, then tells him to sell his possessions. The pericope is one of the most securely attested triple-tradition units, and its parallel structure rules out the suggestion that these are three separate interviews. The divergence is therefore an editorial one, and it falls precisely where Markan priority predicts: on the wording and ordering of the commandment list.

Mark 10:19 reads: 'Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Defraud not, Honour thy father and thy mother.' Two features are striking. First, Mark places adultery before murder, inverting the Masoretic order (Exod 20:13-16; Deut 5:17-20) where murder comes first. Interestingly, this adultery-first sequence matches the order found in the major LXX manuscripts (Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) at Deut 5 and in Luke's parallel, in Romans 13:9, James 2:11, and Philo — suggesting a recognized Hellenistic-Jewish catechetical tradition rather than a slip. Second, Mark inserts 'Defraud not' (mē aposterēsēs), which is not part of the Decalogue at all. Joel Marcus in the Anchor Yale Bible Mark treats it as reflecting either an expansion of the tenth commandment on coveting (the LXX of Deut 24:14 uses the cognate verb of withholding a laborer's wage) or an echo of Sirach 4:1. Because the wealthy man's besetting sin turns out to be his possessions, the addition is thematically pointed: Mark frames defrauding as the live moral issue.

Matthew 19:18-19 cleans Mark up. He drops the non-Decalogue 'defraud not,' restores something nearer the canonical order, and appends 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' (Lev 19:18) as a climactic sixth item. This is characteristic Matthean redaction: Davies and Allison note that Matthew repeatedly elevates the love command (cf. Matt 22:39-40, where it becomes one of the two commandments on which 'all the law and the prophets' hang). The addition telescopes the rich-man episode forward into Matthew's later Great Commandment debate, giving the Gospel a coherent ethical spine. 'Love thy neighbour' is not in Mark or Luke here; it is Matthew's theological signature.

Luke 18:20 shortens the list to five and tightens the order toward the standard sequence, omitting both 'defraud not' and the love command. Fitzmyer reads this as Luke's habitual stylistic compression of Markan material. The result is three lists that diverge in length, order, and content at the sixth slot — neighbor-love (Matthew), parental honor (Mark), or nothing (Luke).

The standard harmonization, found in Archer and in Blomberg's NAC Matthew, is that Jesus gave a partial, representative selection that each evangelist reports loosely, none claiming a verbatim transcript. That is true as far as it goes, and it correctly identifies that no list purports to be exhaustive. But it does not address the actual data point: the same source material has been reordered and supplemented in divergent directions. The 'different occasions' move fails outright because the surrounding narrative is demonstrably the single Markan pericope, edited. What remains is ordinary redaction — Matthew and Luke reshaping Mark to serve distinct catechetical and theological aims. This is not an error so much as a window into how the evangelists handled tradition. Verdict: harmonizable as to the historical gist (no list claims completeness), but the divergence is real and is best explained as redaction, not as three independent reports.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: None of the three lists claims to be an exhaustive transcript; Jesus plausibly cited a representative selection of the second-table commandments, and each evangelist reproduced it loosely. The wording and ordering differences are then explained by ordinary redaction of a common Markan source rather than by factual conflict — though the divergent sixth item remains a genuine editorial difference.

entries.question: Who asked Jesus for the best seats in heaven?
entries.summary: In Mark 10:35-37, James and John themselves come to Jesus and ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory. In Matthew 20:20-21, the mother of Zebedee's sons does the asking on their behalf. Same Markan pericope, same request, same place in the narrative — but the petitioner has changed from the disciples to their mother.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest examples of Matthean redaction softening an embarrassing tradition in Mark. Mark's James and John look greedy and obtuse — they've just heard Jesus predict his passion for the third time, and their response is to angle for the best seats. Matthew, writing later and trying to protect the reputations of the apostles who will become the pillars of the church, shifts the request to their mother. The disciples are still present and still implicated (Jesus answers *them*, in the plural, in Matt 20:22), but the actual ask comes from a third party. Davies and Allison in the ICC Matthew straightforwardly treat this as redactional embarrassment-management — Matthew is consistently more protective of the Twelve than Mark is. Joel Marcus in AYB Mark concurs. The apologist response — that both happened, the mother spoke first and then the sons spoke for themselves, or vice versa — has to invent a narrative neither evangelist tells. Matt 20:22 has Jesus replying directly to the sons ('ye know not what ye ask'), which only makes sense if they were doing the asking, but Matthew has *just* told us their mother did. The textual seam shows. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, family delegations were a thing in honor-shame culture, and a mother lobbying for her sons is plausible Mediterranean social behavior — Bruce Malina's work on this is solid. But that doesn't explain why Mark, the earlier source, doesn't mention her. The simpler explanation is editorial: Matthew added the mother to shield the apostles. That is of course an inference from redaction, but it's the parsimonious one.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is among the cleanest demonstrations in the triple tradition of Matthew editing Mark to protect the reputation of the Twelve. In Mark 10:35-37, James and John themselves approach Jesus with a blunt, self-serving request — 'Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.' The placement is pointed: it follows immediately on Jesus' third and most detailed passion prediction (Mark 10:32-34), so the brothers' jockeying for status reads as spectacular incomprehension. Mark's portrait of the disciples is consistently unflattering — they fail to understand the parables (4:13), misread the feedings (8:17-21), and here grasp for thrones while their master speaks of crucifixion.

Matthew 20:20-21 reassigns the request to 'the mother of Zebedee's children.' The disciples are not exonerated entirely — they remain present, and crucially Jesus answers them, not her: 'Ye know not what ye ask' (Matt 20:22) is plural in the Greek (oidate, aiteisthe), and the following 'Are ye able to drink of the cup' is addressed to the sons. This grammatical seam is the tell. Matthew has interposed the mother as the speaker in v. 21, yet his source's dialogue, which he retains in v. 22, still has Jesus replying to the brothers. The editorial insertion left a visible joint.

This fits a documented Matthean tendency. Davies and Allison, in the ICC, treat the shift to the mother as redactional management of an embarrassing tradition, and they situate it within Matthew's broader rehabilitation of the disciples (compare Matthew's softening of Mark's harsh 'they understood not' into 'then understood they,' Matt 16:12; 17:13). Joel Marcus concurs that Mark's version is the more difficult and hence more original, and that the mother is a Matthean addition. The criterion of embarrassment cuts in Mark's favor: a request that makes the future pillars of the church look greedy is unlikely to have been invented, and is exactly the sort of thing a later evangelist would want to soften.

The apologetic harmonization holds that both happened — the mother spoke first and the sons seconded the request, or vice versa — so each Gospel records a different moment of one episode. Bruce Malina's work on the collectivist, dyadic personality of Mediterranean antiquity gives this real social plausibility: a mother lobbying on her sons' behalf, with the sons fully complicit, is entirely at home in an honor-shame family system, and it would explain why Jesus answers the sons even though the mother spoke. This is the strongest form of the harmonization and should be granted its due weight.

But it does not explain the source data. Mark, the earlier account, knows nothing of the mother; if she were historically the petitioner, her omission from the earlier source and her appearance only in the later one is the reverse of what we would expect. The parsimonious explanation is editorial: Matthew added her to deflect the discreditable ambition away from James and John. The harmonization can save the historicity of an underlying family scene, but it cannot account for why the tradition develops in precisely the direction that protects the apostles. Verdict: the surface contradiction is harmonizable in principle, but the textual seam and the redactional pattern make Matthean editing the better explanation of the change in petitioner.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: In a collectivist honor-shame culture a mother could petition on her sons' behalf with their full complicity, so both 'the mother asked' and 'the sons asked' can describe one family delegation — which also explains why Jesus answers the sons in the plural. This saves the historicity of an underlying scene, but the absence of the mother from the earlier Markan source and Matthew's documented protection of the Twelve make redaction the more economical account of the difference.

entries.question: Was Jesus a ransom for many or for all?
entries.summary: Matthew 20:28 and Mark 10:45 have Jesus give his life as a *lytron anti pollōn* — a ransom for many. 1 Timothy 2:6 says he gave himself a *antilytron hyper pantōn* — a ransom for all. One says many, the other says all. Whether the atonement is universal or limited rides on which Greek word you read.
entries.commentary: This is the textual fault line that runs through the entire Reformed-Arminian debate on the extent of the atonement. Calvinist readers like John Owen in *The Death of Death in the Death of Christ* lean hard on Mark 10:45's *pollōn* (many) and argue the Pastoral 'all' really means 'all kinds of people' or 'all the elect.' Arminian and Wesleyan readers do the reverse, reading the Synoptic 'many' as a Semitism that includes everyone. The harmonization most modern commentators reach for is the Semitism argument: Joachim Jeremias in *The Eucharistic Words of Jesus* famously argued that *rabbim* in Aramaic and Hebrew functions inclusively rather than exclusively — 'the many' as 'the great multitude,' i.e. everyone. Isaiah 53:11-12, the Suffering Servant background Mark 10:45 is clearly echoing, uses *rabbim* in that inclusive sense. That's the steel-man case for harmony. The trouble is that even granting Jeremias the Semitism move, the Greek word *pollōn* in Mark and Matthew is the standard exclusive-of-some word in Greek — and the Pastor of 1 Timothy felt the need to change it to *pantōn*. That change is itself evidence the early church saw a problem with *pollōn* and corrected toward universalism. Whether 1 Timothy was written by Paul (mainstream critical view: deutero-Pauline, late first century — see Raymond Brown's *Introduction to the New Testament*) or by Paul himself, the rewording is editorial. So the contradiction is real at the level of the Greek text even if the underlying theology can be massaged toward harmony. Take your pick: the synoptic Jesus says many, the Pastor says all, and the difference matters enough that fifteen centuries of soteriology have been fought over it.

commentary_out.commentary:
The contrast is lexical and theological. Matt 20:28 and Mark 10:45 have the Son of Man give his life lytron anti pollōn — 'a ransom for many.' 1 Tim 2:6 has Christ give himself antilytron hyper pantōn — a 'ransom for all.' Two prepositional objects, pollōn (many) and pantōn (all), have anchored fifteen centuries of debate over the extent of the atonement.

The Synoptic logion is steeped in Isaiah 53. The Suffering Servant 'bare the sin of many' (rabbim, Isa 53:12) and 'shall... justify many' (53:11), and Mark 10:45's combination of vicarious death and 'the many' is widely read as a deliberate echo. This supplies the strongest harmonizing argument, classically advanced by Joachim Jeremias in The Eucharistic Words of Jesus: in Hebrew and Aramaic ha-rabbim ('the many') functions inclusively, denoting 'the great multitude,' i.e. all, rather than 'many as opposed to all' in the exclusive Greek sense. On this reading 'ransom for many' and 'ransom for all' are not two different scopes but the same scope expressed in Semitic and Hellenistic idiom. The Qumran community even used ha-rabbim as a self-designation for the whole congregation, supporting the inclusive force. This is the steel-man for harmony, and it is a serious philological case.

The theological stakes are why it matters. Reformed exegetes such as John Owen in The Death of Death in the Death of Christ press Mark 10:45's pollōn to support a definite, limited atonement, reading the Pastoral pantōn as 'all kinds' or 'all the elect.' Arminian and Wesleyan readers run the inverse, taking the Synoptic 'many' as the inclusive Semitism Jeremias described. The same two words are thus marshaled in opposite directions.

The harmonization carries real weight but does not fully dissolve the tension. Even granting Jeremias the Semitic inclusive sense of the underlying tradition, the Greek of Mark and Matthew reads pollōn, the ordinary Greek word that can imply 'many but not all,' while the author of 1 Timothy chose antilytron hyper pantōn — adding the intensive prefix anti- and substituting the unambiguous pantōn. That substitution is itself evidence that an early Christian writer perceived the Synoptic formulation as susceptible to a restrictive reading and moved to forestall it by stating universality outright. The direction of development runs toward explicit universalism. On the mainstream critical view 1 Timothy is deutero-Pauline, composed late in the first century or early in the second (so Raymond Brown's Introduction to the New Testament, with the Pastorals' distinctive vocabulary, ecclesiology, and church order); on that view the rewording reflects a later theological clarification. Even if one holds to Pauline authorship, the choice of pantōn over pollōn remains a deliberate authorial decision.

So the underlying soteriology can plausibly be harmonized — both texts may intend a universally sufficient ransom — but the surface wording diverges in a way that has been theologically consequential. The contradiction is real at the level of the Greek text even where it softens at the level of intended meaning. Verdict: largely harmonizable via the Isaianic rabbim background, but the lexical shift from pollōn to pantōn is a genuine and theologically loaded difference, not a mere stylistic variant.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Synoptic 'for many' (pollōn) echoes Isaiah 53's rabbim, which in Hebrew/Aramaic carries an inclusive sense ('the great multitude' = all), so 'ransom for many' and 'ransom for all' can express the same intended scope in different idioms. This reconciles the underlying soteriology, but the deliberate Greek shift from pollōn to pantōn in 1 Timothy remains a real, theologically weighted difference in wording.

issues.problem: The commentary asserts the substitution of pantōn for pollōn 'is itself evidence that an early Christian writer perceived the Synoptic formulation as susceptible to a restrictive reading and moved to forestall it.' This treats 1 Tim 2:6 as a deliberate redaction/correction OF the Synoptic ransom logion. Mainstream scholarship (incl. Marshall, Mounce) regards 1 Tim 2:6 as an independent reformulation of the ransom tradition (antilytron is a distinct, possibly traditional formula), not as the author editing Mark 10:45. Presenting it as a directional 'correction toward universalism' of the Markan saying overstates the literary dependence and risks strawmanning the relationship. This is a stronger claim than the source-critical evidence supports.
issues.correction: Reframe: the author of 1 Timothy draws on a shared ransom tradition and chooses the explicitly universal pantōn; this reflects the Pastorals' universalist soteriology (cf. 1 Tim 2:4; 4:10) rather than a demonstrable editorial 'correction' of the Synoptic logion. Note that direct literary dependence of 1 Tim 2:6 on Mark/Matthew is not established.

issues.problem: The text says antilytron adds 'the intensive prefix anti-.' The anti- in antilytron is not 'intensive' — it carries the sense of 'in place of / in exchange for' (substitutionary), corresponding to the anti pollōn ('in place of many') of the Synoptic phrase. Calling it intensive is a minor lexical mischaracterization.

entries.question: On the day that Jesus rode into Jerusalem, did Jesus ask his disciples to get one animal or two?
entries.summary: Matthew 21:1-7 has Jesus dispatch two disciples to fetch *an ass and her colt*, and the disciples bring back both animals; Matthew even depicts Jesus sitting on the garments laid across both. Mark 11:1-7 and Luke 19:28-35 mention only a single colt. John 12:14 has Jesus find a young ass himself, without dispatching anyone. One Triumphal Entry, four different vehicles.
entries.commentary: Matthew's two-animal version is a textbook case of an evangelist over-literalizing a Hebrew prophecy. The Zechariah 9:9 oracle Matthew is explicitly citing — 'thy King cometh unto thee, lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass' — uses standard Hebrew synonymous parallelism, where the same animal is named twice in different terms. Zechariah is talking about one donkey, described two ways. Matthew, reading the Greek of the LXX where the parallelism is preserved as 'an ass and a colt,' apparently took it as two separate animals and adjusted his narrative accordingly. Davies and Allison in the ICC are explicit: 'Matthew has misunderstood the Hebrew parallelism.' Joel Marcus calls it 'over-literal exegesis.' R. T. France, who is generally sympathetic to Matthew's reliability, concedes the parallelism point and tries to rescue the situation by suggesting the mother donkey was brought along to keep the unbroken colt calm — a plausible animal-handling note but one Matthew never makes. The apologist harmonization typically runs along France's lines or argues that Mark and Luke 'simplified' to one animal. The problem with the simplification argument is that Mark and Luke are *earlier* than Matthew in the consensus chronology, so they aren't simplifying Matthew — Matthew is *complicating* them. The simpler reading is that the Synoptic tradition knew one animal, Zechariah's parallelism got read literally somewhere in Matthean redaction, and a second donkey appeared in the narrative to fit the prophecy. That is of course an inference from redaction-critical method, but the alternative is to posit that Jesus deliberately rode two animals simultaneously to fulfill a misreading of Zechariah. John, meanwhile, sidesteps the whole disciple-dispatch tradition by having Jesus find the donkey himself — a separate redactional path. Take your pick: Matthew misread the Hebrew, or Jesus straddled two donkeys.

commentary_out.commentary:
The four accounts produce four configurations: Matthew 21:1-7 has Jesus send for *an ass and her colt* and the disciples bring both, with garments laid 'on them'; Mark 11:1-7 and Luke 19:28-35 mention a single colt (πῶλος) on which no one has sat; John 12:14 has Jesus himself find a young ass, with no dispatch of disciples at all. The crux is Matthew's two animals, and the mechanism is well understood.

Matthew alone supplies the explicit fulfillment citation of Zechariah 9:9 (Matt 21:4-5): 'Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass.' The Hebrew of Zech 9:9 reads ʿal-ḥămôr wĕʿal-ʿayir ben-ʾătōnôt — 'on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a she-donkey.' This is textbook synonymous parallelism: the second line restates the first, naming one animal in two ways, exactly as Hebrew poetry routinely doubles a single referent (cf. the waw of explication, 'even a colt'). Zechariah envisions one donkey. The LXX preserves the two nouns (ἐπὶ ὑποζύγιον καὶ πῶλον) without flagging the parallelism, and Matthew — citing a form close to the LXX/MT — appears to have read the two terms as two beasts and reshaped his narrative to match, producing a mother and her colt and the awkward plural 'on them.' Davies and Allison state it flatly: Matthew has misunderstood the Hebrew parallelism. Marcus calls it over-literal exegesis. This is consistent with Matthew's broader fulfillment-citation technique, where narrative details are at times generated to satisfy the cited prophecy.

The strongest harmonizing rescue is R. T. France's: the mother was led along to settle the unbroken colt — a genuine animal-handling reality, since a colt 'whereon never man sat' (Mark 11:2) would be calmer beside its dam. France, sympathetic to Matthew's reliability, concedes the parallelism point but argues the second donkey could be historical even if Matthew's prophetic framing is over-literal. The note is plausible, but Matthew never says this; the text presents the second animal as prophecy-fulfillment, not herd management, and Matthew's 'sat upon them' implies the evangelist pictures both as mounts, not one as an escort. The alternative apologetic line — that Mark and Luke 'simplified' two animals to one — collapses on chronology: under Markan priority Mark and Luke are *earlier*, so Matthew is not being simplified by them; he is complicating their single colt.

The most economical reading therefore credits the Synoptic tradition with one animal, locates the doubling in Matthean redaction driven by the Zechariah citation, and treats John as a separate strand that bypasses the disciple-dispatch tradition entirely. On the historical question — how many animals did Jesus ride — the tension largely dissolves: three of four Gospels say one, and Matthew's second beast is the residue of a citation technique, not independent testimony. What does not dissolve is the discrepancy at the level of the *narrated* text: Matthew's two against the others' one is a real difference, even if its cause is exegetical rather than evidentiary. Verdict: harmonizable at the level of the event (one donkey), with Matthew's narrative count an artifact of over-literal prophecy fulfillment.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The underlying event was one animal: the apparent two-donkey contradiction is a known feature of Matthew's over-literal reading of the synonymous parallelism in Zechariah 9:9, an artifact of fulfillment-citation redaction rather than a claim about the historical entry. Mark, Luke, and John agree on one animal, dissolving the substance of the tension even as Matthew's narrative count stands at odds with theirs.

issues.problem: The commentary cites the Hebrew of Zech 9:9 as 'ʿal-ḥămôr wĕʿal-ʿayir ben-ʾătōnôt.' The MT reads 'ʿal-ḥamor wĕʿal-ʿayir ben-ʾatonot' — but the transliteration as given is essentially correct (the construct chain ben-ʾatonot, 'foal of she-donkeys'). However, the LXX citation is imprecise: the commentary gives the LXX of Zech 9:9 as 'ἐπὶ ὑποζύγιον καὶ πῶλον,' but the actual LXX reads 'ἐπιβεβηκὼς ἐπὶ ὑποζύγιον καὶ πῶλον νέον' (with πῶλον νέον). More importantly, Matthew 21:5 does NOT quote the LXX form here; Matthew's citation ('ἐπὶ ὄνον καὶ ἐπὶ πῶλον υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου') diverges from the LXX, which is itself a noted text-critical point. The commentary's claim that Matthew cites 'a form close to the LXX/MT' glosses over the fact that Matthew's wording is distinctive and does not match the LXX of Zechariah.
issues.correction: Note that Matthew's citation in 21:5 has its own distinctive wording (ὄνον ... πῶλον υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου) that does not simply reproduce the LXX; the over-literal doubling arises from Matthew's reading of the two-noun parallelism however mediated, not from quoting the LXX verbatim.

issues.problem: The commentary references 'the waw of explication, even a colt' as an interpretive gloss on Zech 9:9. While the waw-explicative reading of the parallelism is a legitimate grammatical observation, presenting it as a settled feature is slightly overstated since Hebrew poetic parallelism here is standard synonymous parallelism rather than strictly a waw-explicativum construction. Minor nuance.
issues.correction: Frame the waw as one way of construing the parallelism rather than a fixed grammatical category.
